title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: The Rent of Land

Rent, understood as the price paid for the use of land, is naturally the highest sum the tenant can manage to pay given the land's actual condition. When the terms of a lease are worked out, the landlord tries to leave the tenant no larger share of the produce than what will keep up the capital he draws his seed from, pay for the labour, and buy and maintain the cattle and other farming equipment, along with the ordinary profits that farming capital earns in that neighbourhood. That is plainly the smallest share the tenant can settle for without taking a loss, and the landlord rarely intends to leave him any more. Whatever portion of the produce, or what comes to the same thing, whatever portion of its price, exceeds this share, the landlord naturally tries to keep for himself as the rent of his land, and that is clearly the most the tenant can afford to pay given the land's actual condition. Sometimes the landlord's generosity, and more often his ignorance, leads him to accept somewhat less than this portion; and sometimes too, though more rarely, the tenant's ignorance leads him to agree to pay somewhat more, or to make do with somewhat less, than the ordinary profits of farming capital in the neighbourhood. Even so, this portion can still be regarded as the natural rent of land, the rent at which land is naturally meant, for the most part, to be let.

You might suppose that the rent of land is often nothing more than a reasonable profit or interest on the capital the landlord has spent improving it. On some occasions that may be partly true, but it can scarcely ever be more than partly true. The landlord demands a rent even for unimproved land, and the supposed interest or profit on the cost of improvement is generally added on top of this original rent. Besides, those improvements are not always made with the landlord's capital; sometimes they are made with the tenant's. Yet when the lease comes up for renewal, the landlord commonly demands the same increase in rent as if he had made all the improvements himself.

Sometimes he demands rent for something entirely beyond any human power to improve. Kelp is a kind of seaweed which, when burned, yields an alkaline salt useful for making glass and soap and for several other purposes. It grows in several parts of Great Britain, especially in Scotland, only on rocks that lie within the high-water mark, which are covered by the sea twice a day, so that its yield was never increased by any human effort. Yet the landlord whose estate borders a kelp shore of this sort demands a rent for it just as he does for his cornfields.

The sea around the Shetland islands is unusually rich in fish, which make up a large part of what the inhabitants live on. But to make use of what the water yields, they need a dwelling on the nearby land. The landlord's rent is set in proportion not to what the farmer can earn from the land alone, but to what he can earn from the land and the water together. Part of it is paid in sea-fish, and that country provides one of the very few cases in which rent forms part of the price of that commodity.

The rent of land, then, considered as the price paid for the use of the land, is naturally a monopoly price. It bears no relation at all to what the landlord may have spent improving the land, or to what he could afford to accept, but only to what the farmer can afford to give.

Only those parts of the land's produce can ordinarily be brought to market whose usual price is enough to cover the capital that must be used to bring them there, along with its ordinary profits. If the usual price is more than this, the surplus naturally goes to the rent of the land. If it is no more, the commodity can be brought to market but yields the landlord no rent. Whether the price is more or not depends on demand.

For some parts of the land's produce, the demand must always be high enough to yield a price greater than what is needed to bring them to market; for others, the demand may or may not be high enough to yield this greater price. The first kind must always yield a rent to the landlord. The second kind sometimes does and sometimes does not, depending on the circumstances.

Notice, then, that rent enters into the price of commodities in a different way from wages and profit. High or low wages and profit are the cause of high or low prices; high or low rent is the result of them. A commodity's price is high or low because high or low wages and profit must be paid to bring it to market. But it yields a high rent, a low rent, or no rent at all because its price is a great deal more, or only a little more, or no more, than what is enough to pay those wages and profit.

This chapter will fall into three parts, taking up: first, those parts of the land's produce that always yield some rent; second, those that sometimes do and sometimes do not yield rent; and third, the variations that naturally occur, at different stages of improvement, in the relative value of these two different kinds of raw produce, compared both with each other and with manufactured goods.
Part I. — Of the Produce of Land which always affords Rent.

Since men, like all other animals, naturally multiply in proportion to the means of supporting them, there is always more or less demand for food. Food can always buy or command a greater or smaller quantity of labour, and someone can always be found willing to do something to get it. The quantity of labour it can buy is not always equal to what it could support if managed in the most economical way, because labour is sometimes paid high wages; but food can always buy as much labour as it can support, at the rate at which that kind of labour is commonly supported in the neighbourhood.

But land, in almost any setting, produces more food than is enough to support all the labour needed to bring it to market, even in the most generous way in which that labour is ever supported. The surplus is also always more than enough to replace the capital that employed that labour, along with its profits. So something always remains as a rent for the landlord.

The most barren moors in Norway and Scotland produce some kind of pasture for cattle, whose milk and offspring are always more than enough not only to support all the labour of tending them and to pay the farmer or the owner of the herd or flock his ordinary profit, but also to yield the landlord some small rent. The rent rises in proportion to how good the pasture is. The same area of ground not only feeds more cattle, but because they are kept within a smaller space, less labour is needed to tend them and gather what they produce. The landlord gains in both ways: from the larger produce, and from the smaller amount of labour that must be supported out of it.

The rent of land varies not only with its fertility, whatever its produce, but also with its location, whatever its fertility. Land near a town yields a higher rent than equally fertile land in a distant part of the country. Cultivating the one may cost no more labour than the other, but it always costs more to bring the produce of the distant land to market. So more labour must be supported out of it, and the surplus from which both the farmer's profit and the landlord's rent are drawn must be smaller. But in remote parts of the country the rate of profit, as has already been shown, is generally higher than near a large town. A smaller share of this reduced surplus, therefore, must go to the landlord.

Good roads, canals, and navigable rivers, by reducing the cost of carriage, bring the remote parts of the country more nearly onto a level with those near the town. For that reason they are the greatest of all improvements. They encourage the cultivation of remote districts, which must always make up the widest circle of the country. They benefit the town by breaking down the monopoly held by the countryside in its immediate neighbourhood. They even benefit that immediate countryside. Though they bring some rival goods into the old market, they also open many new markets to its produce. Monopoly, moreover, is a great enemy of good management, which can only become universal through the free and general competition that forces everyone to adopt it in self-defence. It is no more than fifty years ago that some of the counties near London petitioned Parliament against extending the turnpike roads into the more distant counties. Those remoter counties, they claimed, would be able, thanks to cheaper labour, to undersell them with grass and corn in the London market, and so would cut their rents and ruin their farming. Yet their rents have risen, and their farming has improved, since that time.

A cornfield of moderate fertility produces far more food for human beings than the best pasture of the same size. Its cultivation requires much more labour, but the surplus left after replacing the seed and supporting all that labour is likewise much greater. So even if a pound of butcher's meat were never reckoned worth more than a pound of bread, this larger surplus would everywhere be of greater value and would form a larger fund for both the farmer's profit and the landlord's rent. It seems to have done so everywhere in the crude early stages of farming.

But the relative values of these two kinds of food, bread and butcher's meat, differ greatly at different stages of agriculture. In its crude beginnings, the unimproved wilds, which then make up by far the greater part of the country, are all given over to cattle. There is more butcher's meat than bread, so bread is the food most competed for and consequently fetches the highest price. At Buenos Aires, Ulloa tells us, four reals, twenty-one and a half pence sterling, was forty or fifty years ago the usual price of an ox chosen from a herd of two or three hundred. He says nothing about the price of bread, probably because he found nothing remarkable about it. An ox there, he says, costs little more than the labour of catching it. But corn cannot be grown anywhere without a great deal of labour, and in a country lying on the River Plate, at that time the direct route from Europe to the silver mines of Potosi, the money price of labour could be very cheap. It is otherwise once cultivation has spread over the greater part of the country. Then there is more bread than butcher's meat. The competition shifts direction, and the price of butcher's meat comes to exceed that of bread.

As cultivation spreads, moreover, the unimproved wilds become too small to meet the demand for butcher's meat. A large part of the cultivated land must be used for rearing and fattening cattle, so their price must be enough to pay not only the labour of tending them but also the rent the landlord and the profit the farmer could have drawn from such land used for tillage. Cattle reared on the most uncultivated moors, when brought to the same market, sell, in proportion to their weight or quality, at the same price as those reared on the most improved land. The owners of those moors gain by this and raise the rent of their land in proportion to the price of their cattle. It is no more than a century ago that in many parts of the Scottish Highlands butcher's meat was as cheap as, or cheaper than, even oatmeal bread. The Union opened the English market to Highland cattle. Their usual price is now about three times what it was at the start of the century, and the rents of many Highland estates have tripled or quadrupled in the same period. In almost every part of Great Britain a pound of the best butcher's meat is now generally worth more than two pounds of the best white bread, and in plentiful years it is sometimes worth three or four pounds.

In this way, as improvement advances, the rent and profit of unimproved pasture come to be governed to some extent by the rent and profit of improved pasture, and these in turn by the rent and profit of corn. Corn is an annual crop; butcher's meat is a crop that takes four or five years to grow. Since an acre of land therefore produces far less of the one kind of food than of the other, the smaller quantity must be made up for by the higher price. If it were more than made up for, more cornland would be turned into pasture; and if it were not made up for at all, part of what was in pasture would be brought back into corn.

This equality, however, between the rent and profit of grass and those of corn, between land whose immediate produce is food for cattle and land whose immediate produce is food for men, must be understood to hold only across the greater part of the improved land of a large country. In some particular local situations it is quite otherwise, and the rent and profit of grass are far higher than anything corn can yield.

Thus, near a great town, the demand for milk and for fodder for horses often combines with the high price of butcher's meat to raise the value of grass above what might be called its natural ratio to that of corn. This local advantage obviously cannot be passed on to land farther away.

Particular circumstances have sometimes made certain countries so densely populated that the whole territory, like the land near a great town, has not been enough to produce both the grass and the corn needed to feed the inhabitants. Their land has therefore been used mainly to produce grass, the bulkier commodity and the one that cannot so easily be brought from a great distance, while corn, the food of the bulk of the people, has been mostly imported from abroad. Holland is in this situation today, and a large part of ancient Italy seems to have been so during the prosperity of the Romans. To graze land well, old Cato said, as Cicero reports, was the first and most profitable thing in managing a private estate; to graze it tolerably well, the second; and to graze it badly, the third. Ploughing he ranked only fourth in profit and advantage. Tillage in that part of ancient Italy near Rome must indeed have been greatly discouraged by the distributions of corn frequently made to the people, either free or at a very low price. This corn came from the conquered provinces, several of which, instead of taxes, were required to supply a tenth of their produce to the republic at a fixed price of about sixpence a peck. The low price at which this corn was handed out to the people must have driven down the price of what could be brought to the Roman market from Latium, the ancient territory of Rome, and so must have discouraged its cultivation there.

In an open country too, where the main produce is corn, a well-enclosed piece of grass will often rent higher than any cornfield nearby. It is convenient for maintaining the cattle used to cultivate the corn, and in this case its high rent is paid not so much out of the value of its own produce as out of that of the cornlands cultivated by its means. It is likely to fall if the neighbouring lands are ever fully enclosed. The present high rent of enclosed land in Scotland seems due to the scarcity of enclosure, and will probably last no longer than that scarcity does. The advantage of enclosure is greater for pasture than for corn. It saves the labour of guarding the cattle, which also feed better when not disturbed by a keeper or his dog.

But where there is no local advantage of this kind, the rent and profit of corn, or of whatever else is the common vegetable food of the people, must naturally govern, on land fit for producing it, the rent and profit of pasture.

The use of artificial grasses, turnips, carrots, cabbages, and the other devices found for making a given area of land feed more cattle than it could in natural grass might be expected to reduce somewhat the advantage that, in an improved country, the price of butcher's meat naturally has over that of bread. It seems in fact to have done so; and there is some reason to think that, at least in the London market, the price of butcher's meat relative to that of bread is now a good deal lower than it was at the start of the last century.

In the appendix to his life of Prince Henry, Dr Birch gives an account of the prices of butcher's meat as commonly paid by that prince. He records that the four quarters of an ox, weighing six hundred pounds, usually cost him about nine pounds ten shillings, that is thirty-one shillings and eightpence per hundred pounds in weight. Prince Henry died on 6 November 1612, in the nineteenth year of his age.

In March 1764 there was a parliamentary inquiry into the causes of the high price of provisions at that time. Among other evidence to the same effect, a Virginia merchant testified that in March 1763 he had provisioned his ships with beef at twenty-four or twenty-five shillings the hundredweight, which he regarded as the ordinary price, whereas in that dear year he had paid twenty-seven shillings for the same weight and quality. Yet this high price in 1764 is four shillings and eightpence cheaper than the ordinary price paid by Prince Henry; and it is only the best beef, note, that is fit to be salted for such long voyages.

The price paid by Prince Henry comes to 3⅘d per pound for the whole carcass, coarse and choice pieces together; and at that rate the choice pieces could not have sold retail for less than 4½d or 5d the pound.

In the parliamentary inquiry of 1764, the witnesses gave the price of the choice cuts of the best beef to the consumer as 4d and 4½d the pound, and the coarse cuts generally as somewhere between seven farthings and 2½d or 2¾d; and this, they said, was generally a halfpenny dearer than the same kinds of cuts had usually sold for in the month of March. But even this high price is still a good deal cheaper than we can reasonably suppose the ordinary retail price to have been in Prince Henry's time.
During the first twelve years of the last century, the average price of the best wheat at the Windsor market was £1 18s 3½d the quarter of nine Winchester bushels.
But in the twelve years up to and including 1764, the average price of the same measure of the best wheat at the same market was £2 1s 9½d.
In the first twelve years of the last century, then, wheat appears to have been a good deal cheaper, and butcher's meat a good deal dearer, than in the twelve years up to and including 1764.

In all large countries, most of the cultivated land is used to produce either food for men or food for cattle. The rent and profit of these govern the rent and profit of all other cultivated land. If any particular crop yielded less, the land would soon be turned over to corn or pasture; and if any yielded more, some of the land in corn or pasture would soon be turned over to that crop.

Those crops, indeed, that require either a greater initial outlay to improve the land for them or a greater yearly outlay to cultivate them commonly seem to yield, the one a higher rent, the other a higher profit, than corn or pasture. But this advantage will seldom turn out to amount to more than a reasonable interest on, or compensation for, the extra expense.

In a hop garden, a fruit garden, or a kitchen garden, both the landlord's rent and the farmer's profit are generally higher than in a corn or grass field. But bringing the ground into this condition costs more, so a higher rent becomes due to the landlord. It also calls for more careful and skilful management, so a higher profit becomes due to the farmer. The crop, too, at least in the hop and fruit garden, is more uncertain. Its price must therefore, besides covering all occasional losses, yield something like the profit of insurance. The circumstances of gardeners, generally modest and never more than moderate, may convince us that their great skill is not usually overpaid. Their delightful art is practised by so many rich people for amusement that little money is to be made by those who practise it for profit, because the very people who ought naturally to be their best customers supply themselves with all their most prized produce.

The advantage a landlord gets from such improvements seems never to have been greater than what was enough to cover the original cost of making them. In ancient farming, after the vineyard, a well-watered kitchen garden seems to have been the part of the farm thought to yield the most valuable produce. But Democritus, who wrote on farming about two thousand years ago and was regarded by the ancients as one of the founders of the art, thought it unwise to enclose a kitchen garden. The profit, he said, would not cover the cost of a stone wall; and bricks (sun-dried bricks, I suppose he meant) crumbled in the rain and the winter storms and needed constant repair. Columella, who reports this opinion of Democritus, does not dispute it but proposes a very economical way of enclosing with a hedge of brambles and briars, which he says he had found by experience to be both lasting and impenetrable, though it seems this was not commonly known in Democritus's time. Palladius adopts Columella's view, which Varro had recommended before. In the judgment of those ancient improvers, the produce of a kitchen garden had apparently been little more than enough to pay for the extra cultivation and the cost of watering; for in countries so near the sun it was thought proper, then as now, to have command of a stream of water that could be led to every bed in the garden. Across most of Europe, a kitchen garden is still not thought to deserve a better enclosure than the one Columella recommended. In Great Britain and some other northern countries, the finer fruits cannot be brought to perfection without the help of a wall. Their price in such countries must therefore be enough to cover the cost of building and maintaining what they cannot do without. The fruit-wall often surrounds the kitchen garden, which thus enjoys the benefit of an enclosure that its own produce could seldom pay for.

That the vineyard, when properly planted and brought to perfection, was the most valuable part of the farm seems to have been an unquestioned maxim in ancient agriculture, as it is in modern agriculture throughout all the wine countries. But whether it was worthwhile to plant a new vineyard was a matter of dispute among the ancient Italian farmers, as we learn from Columella. He decides, like a true lover of every curious kind of cultivation, in favour of the vineyard, and tries to show, by comparing profit and expense, that it was a most advantageous improvement. Such comparisons of the profit and expense of new projects, however, are commonly very misleading, and nowhere more so than in agriculture. Had the gain actually made from such plantings been commonly as great as he imagined it could be, there could have been no dispute about it. The same point is still often a matter of controversy in the wine countries today. Their agricultural writers, indeed, being lovers and promoters of intensive cultivation, generally seem inclined to decide with Columella in favour of the vineyard. In France, the eagerness of the owners of old vineyards to prevent the planting of any new ones seems to support their view and to show that those who must have the experience are aware that this kind of cultivation is at present more profitable in that country than any other. At the same time, however, it seems to point to another opinion, that this greater profit can last no longer than the laws that at present restrict the free planting of vines. In 1731 those owners obtained an order of council forbidding both the planting of new vineyards and the renewal of old ones whose cultivation had been interrupted for two years, without special permission from the king, to be granted only after a report from the provincial intendant certifying that he had examined the land and found it incapable of any other crop. The stated reason for this order was the scarcity of corn and pasture and the glut of wine. But if this glut had been real, it would, without any order of council, have effectively prevented the planting of new vineyards by driving the profits of this kind of cultivation below their natural ratio to those of corn and pasture. As for the supposed scarcity of corn caused by the spread of vineyards, corn is nowhere in France more carefully cultivated than in the wine provinces where the land is fit to grow it, as in Burgundy, Guienne, and Upper Languedoc. The many hands employed in the one kind of cultivation necessarily encourage the other by providing a ready market for its produce. To reduce the number of those able to pay for corn is surely a most unpromising way to encourage its cultivation. It is like the policy that would promote agriculture by discouraging manufactures.

The rent and profit of those crops, then, that require either a greater initial outlay to improve the land for them or a greater yearly outlay to cultivate them, though often much higher than those of corn and pasture, are in reality governed by the rent and profit of those common crops whenever they do no more than cover such extraordinary expense.

It does sometimes happen, though, that the amount of land that can be made fit for some particular crop is too small to meet the effective demand. The whole produce can be sold to those willing to pay somewhat more than is enough to cover the whole rent, wages, and profit needed to raise it and bring it to market at their natural rates, or at the rates paid on most other cultivated land. In this case, and only in this case, the surplus part of the price left after covering the whole cost of improvement and cultivation may commonly bear no regular proportion to the like surplus in corn or pasture, but may exceed it to almost any degree; and the greater part of this excess naturally goes to the landlord's rent.

The usual and natural proportion, for instance, between the rent and profit of wine and those of corn and pasture must be understood to hold only for those vineyards that produce nothing but good ordinary wine, the kind that can be grown almost anywhere on any light, gravelly, or sandy soil, and that has nothing to recommend it but its strength and wholesomeness. Only with such vineyards can the ordinary land of the country be brought into competition; with vineyards of a special quality it plainly cannot.

The vine is affected by differences of soil more than any other fruit tree. From some soils it takes a flavour that no cultivation or management, it is supposed, can match on any other. This flavour, real or imagined, is sometimes peculiar to the produce of a few vineyards, sometimes extends over most of a small district, and sometimes over a large part of a great province. The whole quantity of such wines brought to market falls short of the effective demand, that is, the demand of those willing to pay the whole rent, profit, and wages needed to prepare them and bring them to market at the usual rate, the rate paid in ordinary vineyards. The whole quantity can therefore be sold to those willing to pay more, which necessarily raises their price above that of ordinary wine. The difference is greater or smaller according to how far the fashionableness and scarcity of the wine make the buyers compete more or less eagerly. Whatever it is, the greater part of it goes to the landlord's rent. For though such vineyards are generally cultivated more carefully than most others, the high price of the wine seems to be not so much the effect as the cause of this careful cultivation. With so valuable a product, the loss from carelessness is so great that it forces even the most careless to be attentive. A small part of this high price is therefore enough to pay the wages of the extra labour spent on their cultivation and the profits of the extra capital that sets that labour in motion.

The sugar colonies held by the European nations in the West Indies may be compared to those precious vineyards. Their whole produce falls short of Europe's effective demand and can be sold to those willing to pay more than is enough to cover the whole rent, profit, and wages needed to prepare it and bring it to market at the rate commonly paid for any other produce. In Cochin China the finest white sugar generally sells for three piastres the quintal, about thirteen shillings and sixpence of our money, as Mr Poivre tells us in his Voyages d'un Philosophe, a very careful observer of that country's agriculture. What is there called a quintal weighs from a hundred and fifty to two hundred Paris pounds, or a hundred and seventy-five Paris pounds on average, which brings the price of the English hundredweight down to about eight shillings sterling, not a quarter of what is commonly paid for the brown or muscovado sugars imported from our colonies, and not a sixth of what is paid for the finest white sugar. Most of the cultivated land in Cochin China is used to grow corn and rice, the food of the bulk of the people. The respective prices of corn, rice, and sugar there are probably in their natural proportion, the proportion that naturally arises among the different crops on most cultivated land, which repays the landlord and farmer, as nearly as can be reckoned, according to the usual initial cost of improvement and yearly cost of cultivation. But in our sugar colonies the price of sugar bears no such proportion to that of the produce of a rice or corn field in either Europe or America. It is commonly said that a sugar planter expects the rum and molasses to cover the whole cost of his cultivation and his sugar to be all clear profit. If this is true, and I do not claim it is, it is as if a corn farmer expected to cover the cost of his cultivation with the chaff and the straw and to have the grain all as clear profit. We often see companies of merchants in London and other trading towns buy waste land in our sugar colonies, which they expect to improve and cultivate at a profit through factors and agents, despite the great distance and the uncertain returns that come from the poor administration of justice in those countries. Yet nobody will try to improve and cultivate in the same way the most fertile lands of Scotland, Ireland, or the corn provinces of North America, even though, because justice is administered more exactly there, more regular returns might be expected.

In Virginia and Maryland, growing tobacco is preferred to growing corn as the more profitable. Tobacco could be grown with advantage over most of Europe, but in almost every part of Europe it has become a main object of taxation; and collecting a tax from every separate farm in the country where the plant might happen to be grown has been thought more difficult than levying one on its import at the custom-house. For this reason the growing of tobacco has been most absurdly prohibited over most of Europe, which necessarily gives a sort of monopoly to the countries where it is allowed; and since Virginia and Maryland produce the most of it, they share largely, though with some rivals, in the advantage of this monopoly. Growing tobacco, however, seems not to be as profitable as growing sugar. I have never even heard of a tobacco plantation improved and cultivated by the capital of merchants living in Great Britain, and our tobacco colonies send us home no such wealthy planters as we often see arrive from our sugar islands. Although the preference given in those colonies to tobacco over corn suggests that Europe's effective demand for tobacco is not fully supplied, it is probably more nearly supplied than the demand for sugar; and although the present price of tobacco is probably more than enough to pay the whole rent, wages, and profit needed to prepare it and bring it to market at the rate commonly paid on corn land, it must not be so much more as the present price of sugar is. Accordingly, our tobacco planters have shown the same fear of a glut of tobacco that the owners of the old vineyards in France have of a glut of wine. By act of assembly they have limited its cultivation to six thousand plants, supposed to yield a thousandweight of tobacco, for every negro between sixteen and sixty years old. Such a negro, over and above this quantity of tobacco, can manage, they reckon, four acres of Indian corn. To keep the market from being overstocked, they have also sometimes, in plentiful years, burned a certain quantity of tobacco for every negro, as the Dutch are said to do with spices, so Dr Douglas tells us in his Summary, vol. ii, pp. 372, 373, though I suspect he was ill informed. If such violent methods are needed to keep up the present price of tobacco, the advantage of growing it over growing corn, if it still has any, will probably not last long.

It is in this way that the rent of cultivated land whose produce is human food governs the rent of most other cultivated land. No particular crop can long yield less, because the land would at once be put to another use; and if any particular crop commonly yields more, it is because the amount of land that can be made fit for it is too small to meet the effective demand.

In Europe, corn is the main produce of land that serves directly as human food. Except in particular situations, then, the rent of cornland governs in Europe the rent of all other cultivated land. Britain need envy neither the vineyards of France nor the olive groves of Italy. Except in particular situations, their value is governed by that of corn, in which Britain's fertility is not much below that of either of those two countries.

If, in any country, the common and favourite vegetable food of the people were drawn from a plant of which the most ordinary land, with the same or nearly the same cultivation, produced far more than the most fertile land produces of corn, then the landlord's rent, the surplus of food left to him after paying the labour and replacing the farmer's capital along with its ordinary profits, would necessarily be far greater. Whatever the rate at which labour was commonly supported in that country, this greater surplus could always support more of it, and so enable the landlord to buy or command more of it. The real value of his rent, his real power and authority, his command over the necessities and comforts of life that other people's labour could supply him with, would necessarily be far greater.

A rice field produces far more food than the most fertile cornfield. Two crops a year, of thirty to sixty bushels each, are said to be the ordinary yield of an acre. So although growing it takes more labour, a much greater surplus remains after supporting all that labour. In those rice countries, then, where rice is the common and favourite vegetable food of the people and where the cultivators are chiefly fed on it, a greater share of this greater surplus should go to the landlord than in corn countries. In Carolina, where the planters, as in other British colonies, are generally both farmers and landlords, so that rent is mixed up with profit, growing rice is found to be more profitable than growing corn, even though their fields yield only one crop a year and even though, owing to the prevailing customs of Europe, rice is not there the common and favourite vegetable food of the people.

A good rice field is a bog in all seasons, and in one season a bog covered with water. It is unfit for corn, pasture, vineyard, or indeed any other vegetable produce very useful to people; and the lands fit for those purposes are unfit for rice. So even in the rice countries the rent of rice land cannot govern the rent of the other cultivated land, which can never be turned to that crop.

The food produced by a field of potatoes is not less in quantity than that produced by a field of rice, and much greater than that produced by a field of wheat. Twelve thousandweight of potatoes from an acre is not a greater yield than two thousandweight of wheat. The solid nourishment that can be drawn from each of the two plants is not, indeed, quite in proportion to their weight, because of the watery nature of potatoes. But allowing half the weight of this root to go to water, a very generous allowance, such an acre of potatoes will still produce six thousandweight of solid nourishment, three times the quantity produced by the acre of wheat. An acre of potatoes is cultivated at less expense than an acre of wheat, the fallow that usually precedes the sowing of wheat more than making up for the hoeing and other extra cultivation always given to potatoes. Should this root ever become, in any part of Europe, like rice in some rice countries, the common and favourite vegetable food of the people, taking up the same share of the land in tillage that wheat and other grains for human food do at present, the same amount of cultivated land would support far more people; and since the labourers would generally be fed on potatoes, a greater surplus would remain after replacing all the capital and supporting all the labour used in cultivation. A greater share of this surplus, too, would go to the landlord. Population would grow, and rents would rise far above what they are now.

Land fit for potatoes is fit for almost every other useful vegetable. If potatoes took up the same share of cultivated land that corn does now, they would govern, in the same way, the rent of most other cultivated land.

In some parts of Lancashire it is claimed, I have been told, that oatmeal bread is heartier food for working people than wheaten bread, and I have often heard the same doctrine held in Scotland. I am, however, somewhat doubtful of its truth. The common people of Scotland, who are fed on oatmeal, are generally neither so strong nor so good-looking as people of the same rank in England, who are fed on wheaten bread. They neither work so well nor look so well; and since there is no such difference between the people of fashion in the two countries, experience would seem to show that the food of the common people in Scotland is not as suited to the human constitution as that of their counterparts of the same rank in England. But it seems to be otherwise with potatoes. The chairmen, porters, and coal-heavers in London, and those unfortunate women who live by prostitution, perhaps the strongest men and the most beautiful women in the British dominions, are said to come, the greater part of them, from the lowest rank of people in Ireland, who are generally fed on this root. No food can give more decisive proof of its nourishing quality, or of its being especially suited to the health of the human constitution.

It is hard to keep potatoes through the year and impossible to store them like corn for two or three years on end. The fear of not being able to sell them before they rot discourages their cultivation, and is perhaps the chief obstacle to their ever becoming, like bread, the main vegetable food of all the different ranks of people in any large country.
Part II. — Of the Produce of Land, which sometimes does, and sometimes does not, afford Rent.
Human food seems to be the only produce of land that always and necessarily yields some rent to the landlord. Other sorts of produce sometimes do and sometimes do not, depending on the circumstances.
After food, clothing and lodging are the two great wants of mankind.

Land in its original raw state can supply the materials of clothing and lodging to far more people than it can feed. In its improved state it can sometimes feed more people than it can supply with those materials, at least in the form in which they want them and are willing to pay for them. In the one state, then, there is always a glut of these materials, which on that account are often of little or no value. In the other there is often a scarcity, which necessarily raises their value. In the one state, much of them is thrown away as useless, and the price of what is used is reckoned to equal only the labour and expense of fitting it for use, so it can yield the landlord no rent. In the other, they are all used up, and there is often a demand for more than can be had. Someone is always willing to give more for every part of them than is enough to pay the cost of bringing them to market. Their price, therefore, can always yield the landlord some rent.

The skins of the larger animals were the original materials of clothing. Among nations of hunters and shepherds, then, whose food consists chiefly of the flesh of those animals, every man, by getting himself food, also gets himself the materials for more clothing than he can wear. If there were no foreign trade, most of it would be thrown away as worthless. This was probably the case among the hunting nations of North America before Europeans discovered their country; with the Europeans they now exchange their surplus furs for blankets, firearms, and brandy, which gives the furs some value. In the present commercial state of the known world, even the most barbarous nations among whom land property is established have, I believe, some foreign trade of this kind, and find among their wealthier neighbours such a demand for all the clothing materials their land produces, which can be neither worked up nor consumed at home, that it raises their price above the cost of sending them to those wealthier neighbours. So it yields the landlord some rent. When most of the Highland cattle were consumed on their own hills, the export of their hides made up the largest article of that country's trade, and what they were exchanged for added something to the rent of the Highland estates. The wool of England, which in old times could be neither consumed nor worked up at home, found a market in the then wealthier and more industrious country of Flanders, and its price added something to the rent of the land that produced it. In countries no better cultivated than England was then, or than the Scottish Highlands are now, and having no foreign trade, the materials of clothing would obviously be so superabundant that much of them would be thrown away as useless, and none of them could yield the landlord any rent.

The materials of lodging cannot always be carried as far as those of clothing and do not so readily become an object of foreign trade. When they are superabundant in the country that produces them, it often happens, even in the present commercial state of the world, that they are of no value to the landlord. A good stone quarry near London would yield a considerable rent; in many parts of Scotland and Wales it yields none. Plain timber for building is of great value in a populous and well-cultivated country, and the land that produces it yields a considerable rent. But in many parts of North America the landlord would be much obliged to anyone who would carry away the greater part of his large trees. In some parts of the Scottish Highlands the bark is the only part of the wood that, for want of roads and water-carriage, can be sent to market; the timber is left to rot on the ground. When the materials of lodging are so superabundant, the part that is used is worth only the labour and expense of fitting it for use. It yields the landlord no rent, and he generally lets anyone use it who takes the trouble of asking. The demand of wealthier nations, however, sometimes enables him to get a rent for it. The paving of the streets of London has enabled the owners of some barren rocks on the coast of Scotland to draw a rent from what never yielded any before. The woods of Norway and of the Baltic coasts find a market in many parts of Great Britain that they could not find at home, and so yield their owners some rent.

Countries are populous not in proportion to the number of people their produce can clothe and lodge, but in proportion to the number it can feed. Once food is provided, the necessary clothing and lodging are easy to find. But though these are at hand, food may often be hard to find. In some parts of the British dominions, what is called a house can be built by one day's labour of one man. The simplest clothing, the skins of animals, needs rather more labour to dress and prepare for use, but not a great deal. Among savage or barbarous nations, a hundredth part of the whole year's labour, or a little more, will be enough to provide them with such clothing and lodging as satisfy most of the people. The other ninety-nine parts are often no more than enough to provide them with food.

But when, through the improvement and cultivation of land, the labour of one family can provide food for two, the labour of half the society becomes enough to provide food for the whole. The other half, then, or at least the greater part of them, can be employed in providing other things or in satisfying the other wants and fancies of mankind. Clothing and lodging, household furniture, and what is called equipage are the chief objects of most of those wants and fancies. The rich man eats no more food than his poor neighbour. In quality it may differ greatly, and to choose and prepare it may take more labour and skill; but in quantity it is very nearly the same. Yet compare the spacious palace and great wardrobe of the one with the hovel and few rags of the other, and you will see that the difference in their clothing, lodging, and household furniture is almost as great in quantity as in quality. The desire for food is limited in every man by the narrow capacity of the human stomach; but the desire for the comforts and ornaments of building, dress, equipage, and household furniture seems to have no limit or fixed boundary. So those who command more food than they themselves can eat are always willing to exchange the surplus, or what comes to the same thing, the price of it, for gratifications of this other kind. What is over and above satisfying the limited desire is given for the amusement of those desires that cannot be satisfied but seem altogether endless. The poor, in order to get food, exert themselves to gratify these fancies of the rich; and to get it more surely, they compete with one another in the cheapness and excellence of their work. The number of workmen grows with the growing quantity of food, that is, with the growing improvement and cultivation of the land; and since the nature of their work allows the utmost subdivision of labour, the quantity of materials they can work up grows in a far greater proportion than their numbers. Hence arises a demand for every kind of material that human invention can use, either usefully or ornamentally, in building, dress, equipage, or household furniture: for the fossils and minerals in the bowels of the earth, the precious metals, and the precious stones.

In this way food is not only the original source of rent, but every other part of the land's produce that afterwards yields rent derives that part of its value from the improvement in the powers of labour to produce food, brought about by the improvement and cultivation of land.

Those other parts of the land's produce that afterwards yield rent, however, do not always yield it. Even in improved and cultivated countries the demand for them is not always high enough to yield a price greater than is enough to pay the labour and to replace, along with its ordinary profits, the capital that must be used to bring them to market. Whether it is or is not so high depends on various circumstances.
Whether a coal mine, for example, can yield any rent depends partly on its fertility and partly on its situation.

A mine of any kind may be called either fertile or barren according as the quantity of mineral that a given amount of labour can bring from it is greater or smaller than what an equal amount of labour can bring from most other mines of the same kind.
Some coal mines, though well situated, cannot be worked because they are barren. The produce does not pay the cost. They can yield neither profit nor rent.

There are some whose produce is barely enough to pay the labour and to replace, along with its ordinary profits, the capital used in working them. They yield some profit to the undertaker of the work but no rent to the landlord. They can be worked profitably by no one but the landlord, who, being himself the undertaker, gets the ordinary profit on the capital he puts into it. Many coal mines in Scotland are worked in this way and can be worked in no other. The landlord will let no one else work them without paying some rent, and no one can afford to pay any.

Other coal mines in the same country, fertile enough, cannot be worked because of their situation. A quantity of mineral enough to cover the cost of working could be brought from the mine by the ordinary, or even less than the ordinary, amount of labour; but in an inland country, thinly populated and without either good roads or water-carriage, this quantity could not be sold.
Coal is a less pleasant fuel than wood, and is said to be less wholesome too. So the cost of coal, at the place where it is burned, must generally be somewhat less than that of wood.

The price of wood, again, varies with the state of agriculture in nearly the same way, and for exactly the same reason, as the price of cattle. In its crude beginnings, most of every country is covered with wood, which is then a mere nuisance, of no value to the landlord, who would gladly give it to anyone for the cutting. As agriculture advances, the woods are partly cleared by the spread of tillage and partly decay because of the growing number of cattle. These, though they do not increase in the same proportion as corn, which is entirely the product of human effort, still multiply under the care and protection of men, who store up in times of plenty what may keep them in times of scarcity; who, throughout the year, supply them with more food than uncultivated nature provides; and who, by destroying and rooting out their enemies, secure them in the free enjoyment of all that nature provides. Numerous herds of cattle, when allowed to roam through the woods, do not destroy the old trees, but they prevent any young ones from coming up, so that in the course of a century or two the whole forest falls into ruin. The scarcity of wood then raises its price. It yields a good rent, and the landlord sometimes finds he can hardly use his best lands more profitably than in growing plain timber, whose great profit often makes up for the lateness of the returns. This seems to be nearly the state of things at present in several parts of Great Britain, where the profit of planting is found to equal that of either corn or pasture. The advantage a landlord gets from planting can nowhere exceed, at least for any length of time, the rent those crops could yield him; and in a highly cultivated inland country it will often fall not much short of this rent. On the sea-coast of a well-improved country, indeed, if coal can conveniently be had for fuel, it may sometimes be cheaper to bring plain building timber from less cultivated foreign countries than to grow it at home. In the new town of Edinburgh, built within these few years, there is perhaps not a single stick of Scottish timber.

Whatever the price of wood may be, if that of coal is such that the cost of a coal fire is nearly equal to that of a wood one, we may be sure that at that place and in those circumstances the price of coal is as high as it can be. This seems to be so in some inland parts of England, particularly in Oxfordshire, where it is usual, even in the fires of common people, to mix coal and wood together, so that the difference in cost between the two fuels cannot be very great there. Coal, in the coal countries, is everywhere far below this highest price. If it were not, it could not bear the cost of distant carriage by either land or water. Only a small quantity could be sold; and the coal masters and coal owners find it more in their interest to sell a large quantity at a price somewhat above the lowest than a small quantity at the highest. The most fertile coal mine, too, governs the price of coal at all the other mines in its neighbourhood. Both the owner and the undertaker of the work find, the one that he can get a higher rent, the other that he can get a higher profit, by somewhat underselling all their neighbours. Their neighbours are soon forced to sell at the same price, though they can less well afford it, and though it always reduces, and sometimes wholly removes, both their rent and their profit. Some works are abandoned altogether; others can yield no rent and can be worked only by the owner.

The lowest price at which coal can be sold for any length of time is, like that of all other commodities, the price that is barely enough to replace, along with its ordinary profits, the capital that must be used to bring it to market. At a coal mine for which the landlord can get no rent, but which he must either work himself or leave alone entirely, the price of coal must generally be about this price.

Rent, even where coal yields any, generally makes up a smaller share of its price than of the price of most other parts of the raw produce of land. The rent of an estate above ground commonly comes to what is reckoned a third of the gross produce, and it is generally a fixed rent, independent of the occasional variations in the crop. In coal mines, a fifth of the gross produce is a very high rent, a tenth the common rent; and it is seldom a fixed rent, but depends on the occasional variations in the produce. These are so great that in a country where thirty years' purchase is considered a moderate price for a landed estate, ten years' purchase is regarded as a good price for a coal mine.

The value of a coal mine to its owner often depends as much on its situation as on its fertility. The value of a metal mine depends more on its fertility and less on its situation. The coarse metals, and still more the precious ones, when separated from the ore, are so valuable that they can generally bear the cost of a very long land journey and of the most distant sea carriage. Their market is not confined to the countries near the mine but extends to the whole world. The copper of Japan is an article of trade in Europe; the iron of Spain, in that of Chile and Peru. The silver of Peru makes its way not only to Europe but from Europe on to China.

The price of coal in Westmoreland or Shropshire can have little effect on its price at Newcastle, and its price in the Lyonnais can have none at all. The products of such distant coal mines can never be brought into competition with one another. But the products of the most distant metal mines often can be, and in fact commonly are.

So the price of the coarse metals, and even more so of the precious ones, at the world's most productive mines must inevitably affect their price at every other mine. The price of copper in Japan has to influence its price at the copper mines of Europe. The price of silver in Peru, or the amount of labour or other goods it will buy there, has to influence its price not only at the silver mines of Europe but at those of China as well. After the mines of Peru were discovered, most of Europe's silver mines were abandoned. Silver had dropped so far in value that what these mines produced could no longer cover the cost of working them, or repay, with a profit, the food, clothing, lodging, and other necessities consumed in the process. The same thing happened to the mines of Cuba and St Domingo, and even to the old mines of Peru once the mines of Potosi were found. Because the price of every metal at every mine is governed to some degree by its price at the most productive mine in the world that is actually being worked, at most mines it can do little more than pay the cost of working, and it can rarely yield a high rent to the landlord. Rent, then, seems at most mines to make up only a small part of the price of the coarse metals, and an even smaller part of the price of the precious ones. Labour and profit account for most of the price of both.

A sixth of the gross output may be taken as the average rent of the tin mines of Cornwall, the most productive known anywhere in the world, according to the Reverend Mr Borlace, vice-warden of the stannaries. Some mines, he says, yield more, and some yield less. A sixth of the gross output is also the rent of several highly productive lead mines in Scotland.

In the silver mines of Peru, Frezier and Ulloa tell us, the owner often demands nothing from the person working the mine except that he grind his ore at the owner's mill, paying the usual toll or grinding fee. Until 1736, indeed, the king of Spain's tax came to a fifth of the standard silver, and until then this fifth could be regarded as the real rent of most of Peru's silver mines, the richest the world has known. Had there been no tax, this fifth would naturally have gone to the landlord, and many mines could have been worked that were not worked at the time because they could not cover the tax. The duke of Cornwall's tax on tin is reckoned at more than five per cent, or a twentieth of the value; and whatever his share, it too would naturally go to the owner of the mine if tin were duty-free. But if you add a twentieth to a sixth, you find that the whole average rent of the tin mines of Cornwall stood to the whole average rent of the silver mines of Peru as thirteen to twelve. Yet the silver mines of Peru can no longer pay even this low rent, and in 1736 the tax on silver was cut from a fifth to a tenth. Even this lighter tax on silver tempts smuggling more than the twentieth on tin does, and smuggling must be far easier with a precious commodity than with a bulky one. So the king of Spain's tax is said to be very poorly paid, and the duke of Cornwall's very well. Rent, then, probably makes up a larger share of the price of tin at the most productive tin mines than of silver at the most productive silver mines in the world. After the capital used to work these different mines has been replaced, along with its ordinary profit, the remainder left to the owner is evidently greater with the coarse metal than with the precious one.

Nor are the profits of those who run silver mines usually very great in Peru. The same highly respected and well-informed authors tell us that when anyone in Peru sets out to work a new mine, he is universally regarded as a man headed for bankruptcy and ruin, and is shunned and avoided on that account. Mining there, it seems, is viewed just as it is here, as a lottery in which the prizes do not make up for the blanks, though the size of a few prizes tempts many adventurers to throw away their fortunes on such hopeless projects.

Since the sovereign draws a sizeable part of his revenue from the output of the silver mines, however, Peruvian law does everything it can to encourage the discovery and working of new ones. Anyone who discovers a new mine is entitled to mark off two hundred and forty-six feet in length along what he takes to be the direction of the vein, and half that in breadth. He becomes the owner of this stretch of the mine and can work it without paying any acknowledgment to the landlord. The duke of Cornwall's interest has produced a nearly identical rule in that ancient duchy. On waste and unenclosed land, anyone who discovers a tin mine may mark out its limits within a certain extent, which is called bounding a mine. The bounder becomes the real owner of the mine and may either work it himself or lease it to another, without the consent of the landowner, to whom, however, a very small acknowledgment must be paid once it is worked. In both rules, the sacred rights of private property are sacrificed to the supposed interests of public revenue.

Peru gives the same encouragement to the discovery and working of new gold mines, and on gold the king's tax comes to only a twentieth of the standard rental. It was once a fifth, and later a tenth, as with silver; but the work was found unable to bear even the lower of these two taxes. Yet if it is rare, the same authors Frezier and Ulloa say, to find a man who has made his fortune from a silver mine, it is far rarer to find one who has done so from a gold mine. This twentieth seems to be the whole rent paid by most of the gold mines of Chile and Peru. Gold, too, is far more open to smuggling than even silver, both because the metal is worth more for its size and because of the peculiar way nature produces it. Silver is very rarely found pure; like most other metals it is usually combined with some other substance, from which it cannot be separated in paying quantities except by a very laborious and slow process that can only be carried on in purpose-built works, and so lies open to inspection by the king's officers. Gold, by contrast, is almost always found pure. It is sometimes found in fair-sized pieces, and even when mixed in small, almost invisible particles with sand, earth, and other foreign matter, it can be separated from them by a very short and simple process that can be carried out in any private house by anyone with a little mercury. So if the king's tax is poorly paid on silver, it is likely paid far worse on gold, and rent must make up a much smaller part of the price of gold than of silver.

The lowest price at which the precious metals can be sold, or the smallest quantity of other goods for which they can be exchanged over any considerable period, is set by the same principles that fix the lowest ordinary price of all other goods. It is determined by the capital that must ordinarily be employed, and by the food, clothing, and lodging that must ordinarily be consumed, in bringing them from the mine to the market. The price must at least be enough to replace that capital along with the ordinary profit.

Their highest price, however, seems to be set by nothing but the actual scarcity or abundance of the metals themselves. It is not set by the price of any other commodity, in the way the price of coal is capped by the price of wood, beyond which no scarcity can ever push it. Make gold scarce enough and the smallest scrap of it may become more precious than a diamond, exchanging for a greater quantity of other goods.

The demand for these metals arises partly from their usefulness and partly from their beauty. Apart from iron, they are perhaps more useful than any other metal. Because they resist rust and impurity, they are easier to keep clean, and table and kitchen utensils are often more pleasant for being made of them. A silver pot is cleaner than a lead, copper, or tin one, and the same quality makes a gold pot better still than a silver one. Their chief merit, though, lies in their beauty, which makes them especially suited to ornaments of dress and furniture. No paint or dye can give as brilliant a colour as gilding. The merit of their beauty is greatly heightened by their scarcity. For most rich people the chief enjoyment of riches lies in the display of riches, which in their eyes is never so complete as when they appear to possess those unmistakable marks of wealth that nobody else can have. To them, the merit of anything useful or beautiful is greatly heightened by its scarcity, or by the great labour needed to gather any considerable quantity of it, labour that only they can afford to pay for. They are willing to buy such things at a higher price than things far more beautiful and useful but more common. These qualities of usefulness, beauty, and scarcity are the original basis of the high price of these metals, that is, of the large quantity of other goods for which they can be exchanged everywhere. This value existed before, and independently of, their use as coin, and it was the very quality that fitted them for that use. Their use as coin, however, by creating a new demand and reducing the quantity available for other purposes, may afterwards have helped to keep up or raise their value.

The demand for precious stones arises entirely from their beauty. They are of no use except as ornaments, and the merit of their beauty is greatly heightened by their scarcity, or by the difficulty and expense of getting them out of the mine. So wages and profit make up almost the whole of their high price on most occasions. Rent comes in for only a very small share, often for none at all, and only the most productive mines yield any considerable rent. When the jeweller Tavernier visited the diamond mines of Golconda and Visiapour, he was told that the country's ruler, for whose benefit they were worked, had ordered all of them shut except those yielding the largest and finest stones. The rest, it seems, were not worth working for the owner.

Since the prices of both precious metals and precious stones are governed worldwide by their price at the most productive mine, the rent a mine of either kind can yield its owner is in proportion not to its absolute fertility but to what we may call its relative fertility, its superiority over other mines of the same kind. If new mines were discovered as far superior to those of Potosi as those were to the mines of Europe, silver might be cheapened so much that even the mines of Potosi would no longer be worth working. Before the discovery of the Spanish West Indies, the most productive mines in Europe may have yielded their owners as great a rent as the richest mines in Peru do now. Though the quantity of silver was much smaller, it might have exchanged for an equal quantity of other goods, and the owner's share might have let him buy or command an equal quantity of labour or of commodities.
The value both of the output and of the rent, the real revenue they yielded to the public and to the owner alike, might have been the same.

The most abundant mines, whether of precious metals or of precious stones, could add little to the wealth of the world. A product whose value comes mainly from its scarcity is necessarily cheapened by abundance. A set of plate, and the other frivolous ornaments of dress and furniture, could be bought for a smaller quantity of commodities, and this would be the sole advantage the world could draw from such abundance.

It is otherwise with estates above ground. The value both of their output and of their rent is in proportion to their absolute fertility, not their relative fertility. Land that produces a certain quantity of food, clothing, and lodging can always feed, clothe, and house a certain number of people, and whatever the landlord's share, it will always give him a proportionate command over the labour of those people and over the goods that labour can supply him with. The value of the most barren land is not lowered by having the most fertile land nearby. On the contrary, it is generally raised by it. The great number of people supported by the fertile land provide a market for much of what the barren land produces, a market it could never have found among the few its own output could maintain.

Whatever makes land more fertile in producing food raises not only the value of the land improved but also that of much other land, by creating a new demand for its produce. The abundance of food which, thanks to improved land, many people have to dispose of beyond what they can consume themselves, is the great source of demand both for precious metals and precious stones, and for every other convenience and ornament of dress, lodging, household furniture, and equipage. Food not only makes up the main part of the world's riches; it is the abundance of food that gives most of their value to many other kinds of riches. The poor inhabitants of Cuba and St Domingo, when the Spaniards first found them, used to wear little bits of gold as ornaments in their hair and elsewhere on their dress. They seemed to value them as we would value small pebbles of a little more than ordinary beauty, worth picking up but not worth refusing to anyone who asked for them. They handed them to their new guests at the first request, without seeming to think they had given anything very valuable. They were astonished to see the Spaniards' frenzy to get them, and had no idea that anywhere there could be a country where many people had at their disposal so great a surplus of food, food so scarce among themselves that for a very small quantity of those glittering trinkets they would gladly give as much as might support a whole family for years. Had they been able to grasp this, the Spaniards' passion would not have surprised them.
PART III. The Variations in the Proportion Between the Respective Values of the Sort of Produce That Always Yields Rent and the Sort That Sometimes Does and Sometimes Does Not.

The growing abundance of food, as improvement and cultivation increase, must necessarily increase the demand for every part of the produce of land that is not food and can be put to use or ornament. Throughout the whole course of improvement, then, we might expect only one change in the relative values of these two different kinds of produce. The value of the kind that sometimes yields rent and sometimes does not should steadily rise compared with the kind that always yields some rent. As art and industry advance, the materials of clothing and lodging, the useful minerals and materials of the earth, the precious metals and precious stones, should gradually come into greater and greater demand, should gradually exchange for more and more food; or, in other words, should gradually grow dearer and dearer. This, in fact, has been the case with most of these things on most occasions, and would have been the case with all of them on all occasions if particular accidents had not, here and there, raised the supply of some of them even faster than the demand.

The value of a freestone quarry, for example, will necessarily rise as the country around it grows in improvement and population, especially if it is the only quarry in the neighbourhood. But the value of a silver mine, even if there were no other within a thousand miles, will not necessarily rise as the country it sits in improves. The market for the produce of a freestone quarry can rarely reach more than a few miles around it, and the demand must generally be in proportion to the improvement and population of that small district; but the market for the produce of a silver mine may stretch over the whole known world. So unless the world in general is advancing in improvement and population, the demand for silver might not be raised at all by the improvement even of a large country near the mine. And even if the world in general were improving, yet if in the course of that improvement new mines were discovered far more productive than any known before, the demand for silver would necessarily rise, but the supply might rise so much faster that the real price of the metal might gradually fall; that is, any given quantity, a pound weight of it for example, might gradually buy or command less and less labour, or exchange for less and less corn, the labourer's main subsistence.
The great market for silver is the commercial and civilized part of the world.

If the general progress of improvement raised the demand of this market while at the same time the supply did not rise in proportion, the value of silver would gradually rise relative to that of corn. Any given quantity of silver would exchange for more and more corn; or, in other words, the average money price of corn would gradually become cheaper and cheaper.

If, on the other hand, the supply by some accident rose for many years in a greater proportion than the demand, the metal would gradually become cheaper and cheaper; or, in other words, the average money price of corn would, in spite of every improvement, gradually become dearer and dearer.

But if the supply of the metal rose at nearly the same rate as the demand, it would go on buying or exchanging for nearly the same quantity of corn, and the average money price of corn would, in spite of every improvement, stay very nearly the same.

These three cases seem to cover every possible combination of events that can occur in the progress of improvement; and over the four centuries before the present, judging by what has happened in both France and Great Britain, each of these three combinations seems to have occurred in the European market, and nearly in the same order in which I have set them down here.
_A Digression on the Variations in the Value of Silver During the Last Four Centuries._

First Period. In 1350, and for some time before, the average price of a quarter of wheat in England seems to have been reckoned at no less than four ounces of silver, Tower weight, equal to about twenty shillings of our present money. From this price it seems to have fallen gradually to two ounces of silver, equal to about ten shillings of our present money, the price at which we find it reckoned at the start of the sixteenth century, and at which it seems to have stayed reckoned until about 1570.

In 1350, the 25th year of Edward III, what is called the Statute of Labourers was passed. Its preamble complains at length of the insolence of servants who tried to raise their wages on their masters. It therefore orders that all servants and labourers should in future be content with the same wages and liveries (liveries in those days meant not only clothes but provisions) they had been used to receive in the 20th year of the king and the four years before; that on this account their livery-wheat should nowhere be valued higher than tenpence a bushel, and that it should always be the master's choice whether to deliver the wheat or the money. Tenpence a bushel, then, was reckoned in the 25th year of Edward III a very moderate price for wheat, since a special statute was needed to force servants to accept it in place of their usual livery of provisions; and it had been reckoned a reasonable price ten years earlier, in the 16th year of the king, the date the statute refers to. But in the 16th year of Edward III, tenpence contained about half an ounce of silver, Tower weight, and was nearly equal to half a crown of our present money. Four ounces of silver, Tower weight, then, equal to six shillings and eightpence of the money of those times and to nearly twenty shillings of the present, must have been reckoned a moderate price for the quarter of eight bushels.

This statute is surely better evidence of what was reckoned a moderate price for grain in those days than the prices of particular years, which historians and other writers have usually recorded for their extraordinary dearness or cheapness, and from which it is therefore hard to judge what the ordinary price may have been. There are, besides, other reasons to believe that at the start of the fourteenth century, and for some time before, the common price of wheat was not less than four ounces of silver the quarter, and that of other grain in proportion.

In 1309, Ralph de Born, prior of St Augustine's, Canterbury, gave a feast on his installation day, of which William Thorn has preserved not only the bill of fare but the prices of many items. At that feast were consumed: first, fifty-three quarters of wheat, costing nineteen pounds, or seven shillings and twopence a quarter, equal to about twenty-one shillings and sixpence of our present money; second, fifty-eight quarters of malt, costing seventeen pounds ten shillings, or six shillings a quarter, equal to about eighteen shillings of our present money; third, twenty quarters of oats, costing four pounds, or four shillings a quarter, equal to about twelve shillings of our present money. The prices of malt and oats here seem higher than their usual proportion to the price of wheat.

These prices are not recorded for their extraordinary dearness or cheapness, but are mentioned incidentally, as the prices actually paid for large quantities of grain consumed at a feast famous for its magnificence.

In 1262, the 51st year of Henry III, an ancient statute called the assize of bread and ale was revived, which the king says in the preamble had been made in the time of his forebears, some of them kings of England. It is probably, then, at least as old as his grandfather Henry II, and may be as old as the Conquest. It regulates the price of bread according to whatever the price of wheat happens to be, from one shilling to twenty shillings the quarter in the money of those days. But statutes of this kind are generally assumed to provide with equal care for all departures from the middle price, those below it as well as those above. Ten shillings, then, containing six ounces of silver, Tower weight, and equal to about thirty shillings of our present money, must on this assumption have been reckoned the middle price of the quarter of wheat when this statute was first passed, and must have remained so in the 51st year of Henry III. We cannot, therefore, be far wrong in supposing that the middle price was not less than a third of the highest price at which this statute regulates the price of bread, that is, six shillings and eightpence of the money of those days, containing four ounces of silver, Tower weight.

From all these different facts, then, we seem to have some reason to conclude that around the middle of the fourteenth century, and for a considerable time before, the average or ordinary price of the quarter of wheat was not supposed to be less than four ounces of silver, Tower weight.

From about the middle of the fourteenth to the start of the sixteenth century, what was reckoned the reasonable and moderate, that is the ordinary or average, price of wheat seems to have sunk gradually to about half of this price, until at last it fell to about two ounces of silver, Tower weight, equal to about ten shillings of our present money. It went on being valued at this price until about 1570.

In the household book of Henry, the fifth earl of Northumberland, drawn up in 1512, there are two different valuations of wheat. In one it is reckoned at six shillings and eightpence the quarter, in the other at only five shillings and eightpence. In 1512, six shillings and eightpence contained only two ounces of silver, Tower weight, and were equal to about ten shillings of our present money.

From the 25th year of Edward III to the start of Elizabeth's reign, over a span of more than two hundred years, six shillings and eightpence, as several different statutes show, went on being regarded as the so-called moderate and reasonable, that is the ordinary or average, price of wheat. But the quantity of silver contained in that nominal sum was steadily falling over this period, because of alterations made to the coin. Yet the rise in the value of silver had apparently so far made up for the falling quantity of it in the same nominal sum that the legislature did not think it worth bothering about the change.

Thus, in 1436, it was enacted that wheat might be exported without a licence when the price was as low as six shillings and eightpence; and in 1463 it was enacted that no wheat should be imported unless the price was above six shillings and eightpence the quarter. The legislature had supposed that when the price was so low there could be no harm in export, but that when it rose higher it became prudent to allow import. Six shillings and eightpence, then, containing about the same quantity of silver as thirteen shillings and fourpence of our present money (a third less than the same nominal sum contained in Edward III's time), had in those days been regarded as the so-called moderate and reasonable price of wheat.

In 1554, by the 1st and 2nd of Philip and Mary, and in 1558, by the 1st of Elizabeth, the export of wheat was likewise forbidden whenever the price of the quarter exceeded six shillings and eightpence, which by then contained no more than twopence worth more silver than the same nominal sum does now.
