But it had soon been found that to forbid the export of wheat until the price was so very low was in effect to forbid it altogether. So in 1562, by the 5th of Elizabeth, the export of wheat was allowed from certain ports whenever the price of the quarter did not exceed ten shillings, containing nearly the same quantity of silver as the like nominal sum does now. This price, then, had by this time come to be regarded as the so-called moderate and reasonable price of wheat. It agrees closely with the valuation in the Northumberland book of 1512.

That in France the average price of grain was likewise much lower at the end of the fifteenth and start of the sixteenth century than in the two centuries before has been noted by both Mr Dupré de St Maur and the elegant author of the Essay on the Policy of Grain. Its price during the same period had probably sunk in the same way through most of Europe.

This rise in the value of silver relative to corn may have been due entirely to the increased demand for the metal, as improvement and cultivation grew while the supply meanwhile stayed the same as before; or, the demand staying the same as before, it may have been due entirely to the gradual fall in supply, since most of the mines then known in the world were much exhausted and so the cost of working them much increased; or it may have been due partly to the one and partly to the other. At the end of the fifteenth and start of the sixteenth century, most of Europe was moving towards a more settled form of government than it had had for several ages before. Greater security would naturally increase industry and improvement, and the demand for precious metals, like that for every other luxury and ornament, would naturally grow as wealth grew. A greater annual output would need more coin to circulate it, and a greater number of rich people would need more plate and other ornaments of silver. It is natural to suppose, too, that most of the mines then supplying the European market with silver were a good deal exhausted and had become more costly to work. Many of them had been worked since the time of the Romans.

Most of those who have written on the prices of commodities in ancient times, however, have held that from the Conquest, perhaps from Julius Caesar's invasion, down to the discovery of the mines of America, the value of silver was steadily falling. They seem to have been led into this opinion partly by what they happened to observe about the prices of corn and of some other parts of the rude produce of land, and partly by the popular notion that, just as the quantity of silver naturally rises in every country as wealth rises, so its value falls as its quantity rises.
In their observations on the prices of corn, three different circumstances seem often to have misled them.

First, in ancient times almost all rents were paid in kind, in a certain quantity of corn, cattle, poultry, and so on. Sometimes, however, the landlord would stipulate that he should be free to demand of the tenant either the annual payment in kind or a fixed sum of money instead. The price at which the payment in kind was thus exchanged for a fixed sum of money is called in Scotland the conversion price. Since the landlord always has the choice of taking either the goods or the price, it is necessary, for the tenant's safety, that the conversion price should be below rather than above the average market price. In many places, accordingly, it is not much above half this price. Through most of Scotland this custom still holds for poultry, and in some places for cattle. It would probably have held for corn too, had the institution of the public fiars not put an end to it. The fiars are annual valuations, by the judgment of an assize, of the average price of every different sort and quality of grain, according to the actual market price in each different county. This institution made it safe enough for the tenant, and far more convenient for the landlord, to convert, as they call it, the corn rent at whatever happened to be the fiars price of each year, rather than at any fixed price. But the writers who have collected the prices of corn in ancient times seem often to have mistaken what is called in Scotland the conversion price for the actual market price. Fleetwood admits on one occasion that he had made this mistake. But because he wrote his book for a particular purpose, he does not see fit to make this admission until after copying out this conversion price fifteen times. The price is eight shillings the quarter of wheat. This sum in 1423, the year he begins with, contained the same quantity of silver as sixteen shillings of our present money. But in 1562, the year he ends with, it contained no more than the same nominal sum does now.
Second, they have been misled by the careless way in which some ancient statutes of assize were sometimes copied out by lazy scribes, and sometimes, perhaps, actually drafted by the legislature.

The ancient statutes of assize seem always to have begun by setting what the price of bread and ale ought to be when wheat and barley were at their lowest, and then to have gone on step by step to set what it ought to be as the prices of those two grains rose above that lowest level. But the copiers of those statutes seem often to have thought it enough to copy the regulation only as far as the first three or four lowest prices, saving themselves the trouble and judging, I suppose, that this was enough to show what proportion should be kept at all higher prices.

Thus, in the assize of bread and ale of the 51st of Henry III, the price of bread was regulated according to the different prices of wheat, from one shilling to twenty shillings the quarter in the money of those days. But in the manuscripts from which all the different editions of the statutes before Mr Ruffhead's were printed, the copiers had never transcribed this regulation beyond the price of twelve shillings. Several writers, misled by this faulty copy, very naturally concluded that the middle price, or six shillings the quarter, equal to about eighteen shillings of our present money, was the ordinary or average price of wheat at that time.

In the statute of Tumbrel and Pillory, passed about the same time, the price of ale is regulated according to every sixpence rise in the price of barley, from two shillings to four shillings the quarter. But four shillings was not regarded as the highest price barley might often reach in those days, and these prices were given only as an example of the proportion to be kept at all other prices, higher or lower, as we may gather from the statute's last words: "Et sic deinceps crescetur vel diminuetur per sex denarios." The wording is very careless, but the meaning is plain enough: "the price of ale is to be raised or lowered in this way according to every sixpence rise or fall in the price of barley." In drafting this statute the legislature itself seems to have been as careless as the copiers were in transcribing the other.

In an ancient manuscript of the Regiam Majestatem, an old Scottish law book, there is a statute of assize in which the price of bread is regulated according to all the different prices of wheat, from tenpence to three shillings the Scotch boll, equal to about half an English quarter. Three shillings Scotch, at the time this assize is supposed to have been passed, were equal to about nine shillings sterling of our present money. Mr Ruddiman seems (see his Preface to Anderson's Diplomata Scotiae) to conclude from this that three shillings was the highest price wheat ever reached in those days, and that tenpence, a shilling, or at most two shillings were the ordinary prices. But on consulting the manuscript it is plainly clear that all these prices are set down only as examples of the proportion to be kept between the respective prices of wheat and bread. The statute's last words are "reliqua judicabis secundum praescripta, habendo respectum ad pretium bladi": "You shall judge the remaining cases according to what is written above, having regard to the price of corn."

Third, they seem to have been misled too by the very low price at which wheat was sometimes sold in very ancient times, imagining that since its lowest price was then much lower than in later times, its ordinary price must likewise have been much lower. They might have noticed, however, that in those ancient times its highest price was as far above anything ever known in later times as its lowest price was below it. Thus, for 1270, Fleetwood gives us two prices for the quarter of wheat. One is four pounds sixteen shillings of the money of those days, equal to fourteen pounds eight shillings of the present; the other is six pounds eight shillings, equal to nineteen pounds four shillings of our present money. No price found at the end of the fifteenth or start of the sixteenth century comes anywhere near the extravagance of these. The price of corn, though always liable to vary, varies most in those turbulent and disorderly societies where the breakdown of all commerce and communication keeps the plenty of one part of the country from relieving the scarcity of another. In the disorderly England of the Plantagenets, who ruled it from about the middle of the twelfth to nearly the end of the fifteenth century, one district might have plenty while another not far off, its crop destroyed by some accident of the seasons or by the raid of some neighbouring baron, suffered all the horrors of famine; and yet if the lands of some hostile lord lay between them, the one might be unable to give the other the least help. Under the vigorous rule of the Tudors, who governed England through the latter part of the fifteenth and the whole of the sixteenth century, no baron was powerful enough to dare disturb the public peace.

At the end of this chapter the reader will find all the prices of wheat that Fleetwood collected, from 1202 to 1597 inclusive, reduced to present-day money and arranged in order of time into seven divisions of twelve years each. At the end of each division he will also find the average price of the twelve years it contains. Over that long stretch of time, Fleetwood was able to collect the prices of only eighty years, so four years are missing to complete the last twelve. I have therefore added, from the accounts of Eton College, the prices of 1598, 1599, 1600, and 1601. This is the only addition I have made. The reader will see that from the start of the thirteenth century until after the middle of the sixteenth, the average price of each twelve years grows steadily lower and lower, and that towards the end of the sixteenth century it begins to rise again. The prices Fleetwood was able to collect seem to have been mainly those remarkable for extraordinary dearness or cheapness, and I do not claim that any very certain conclusion can be drawn from them. But so far as they prove anything at all, they confirm the account I have been trying to give. Fleetwood himself, however, like most other writers, seems to have believed that throughout this period the value of silver, owing to its growing abundance, was steadily falling. The prices of corn he himself collected certainly do not agree with this opinion. They agree perfectly with that of Mr Dupré de St Maur, and with the one I have been trying to explain. Bishop Fleetwood and Mr Dupré de St Maur are the two authors who seem to have collected the prices of things in ancient times with the greatest diligence and fidelity. It is rather curious that, though their opinions differ so widely, their facts, at least as regards the price of corn, should coincide so exactly.

It is not so much from the low price of corn, however, as from that of some other parts of the rude produce of land, that the most judicious writers have inferred the great value of silver in those very ancient times. Corn, it has been said, being a kind of manufacture, was in those rude ages much dearer in proportion than most other commodities; the comparison meant, I suppose, is with most unmanufactured commodities, such as cattle, poultry, game of all kinds, and so on. That in those times of poverty and barbarism these were proportionably much cheaper than corn is undoubtedly true. But this cheapness was not the effect of the high value of silver; it was the effect of the low value of those commodities. It was not that silver in such times would buy or represent a greater quantity of labour, but that such commodities would buy or represent a much smaller quantity than in times of greater wealth and improvement. Silver must certainly be cheaper in Spanish America than in Europe, in the country where it is produced than in the country it is carried to at the cost of a long journey by both land and sea, plus freight and insurance. Yet twenty-one pence halfpenny sterling was, not many years ago, Ulloa tells us, the price at Buenos Aires of an ox picked from a herd of three or four hundred. Sixteen shillings sterling, Mr Byron tells us, was the price of a good horse in the capital of Chile. In a country naturally fertile but mostly uncultivated, cattle, poultry, game of all kinds, and so on, can be got with very little labour, and so will buy or command but very little. The low money price at which they may be sold is no proof that the real value of silver there is very high, but that the real value of those commodities is very low.
Labour, it must always be remembered, and not any particular commodity or set of commodities, is the real measure of the value of silver and of all other commodities alike.

But in countries almost waste, or only thinly settled, cattle, poultry, game of all kinds, and so on, being the spontaneous products of Nature, are often produced by her in far greater quantities than the inhabitants can consume. In such a state of things the supply commonly exceeds the demand. In different states of society, in different stages of improvement, then, such commodities will represent, or be equal to, very different quantities of labour.

In every state of society, in every stage of improvement, corn is the product of human industry. But the average output of every sort of industry is always matched, more or less exactly, to the average consumption; the average supply to the average demand. Besides, in every different stage of improvement, raising equal quantities of corn from the same soil and climate will, on average, take nearly equal quantities of labour; or, what comes to the same thing, the price of nearly equal quantities of labour. This is because the steady rise in the productive power of labour, in an improved state of cultivation, is more or less offset by the steadily rising price of cattle, the chief instruments of agriculture. On all these grounds, then, we may be sure that equal quantities of corn will, in every state of society and every stage of improvement, more nearly represent, or be equal to, equal quantities of labour than equal quantities of any other part of the rude produce of land. Corn, accordingly, as already noted, is, at all the different stages of wealth and improvement, a more accurate measure of value than any other commodity or set of commodities. At all these different stages, then, we can judge the real value of silver better by comparing it with corn than by comparing it with any other commodity or set of commodities.

Corn, besides, or whatever else is the common and favourite vegetable food of the people, makes up, in every civilized country, the main part of the labourer's subsistence. As agriculture spreads, the land of every country produces a much greater quantity of vegetable than of animal food, and everywhere the labourer lives chiefly on the wholesome food that is cheapest and most plentiful. Butcher's meat, except in the most thriving countries, or where labour is best rewarded, makes up only a small part of his subsistence; poultry a still smaller part, and game none at all. In France, and even in Scotland, where labour is somewhat better rewarded than in France, the labouring poor seldom eat butcher's meat except on holidays and other special occasions. The money price of labour, then, depends far more on the average money price of corn, the labourer's subsistence, than on that of butcher's meat or any other part of the rude produce of land. The real value of gold and silver, then, the real quantity of labour they can buy or command, depends far more on the quantity of corn they can buy or command than on the quantity of butcher's meat or any other part of the rude produce of land.

Such slight observations on the prices of corn or other commodities would probably not have misled so many intelligent authors, had they not been swayed at the same time by the popular notion that, just as the quantity of silver naturally rises in every country as wealth rises, so its value falls as its quantity rises. This notion, however, seems wholly groundless.

The quantity of the precious metals may rise in any country from two different causes: first, from the greater abundance of the mines that supply it; or second, from the greater wealth of the people, from the greater output of their annual labour. The first of these causes is no doubt necessarily linked to a fall in the value of the precious metals; the second is not.

When more abundant mines are discovered, a greater quantity of the precious metals is brought to market; and since the quantity of the necessaries and conveniences of life they must be exchanged for is the same as before, equal quantities of the metals must be exchanged for smaller quantities of commodities. So far, then, as the rise in the quantity of the precious metals in any country comes from the greater abundance of the mines, it is necessarily linked to some fall in their value.

When, on the contrary, the wealth of a country rises, when the annual output of its labour grows steadily greater, more coin becomes necessary to circulate a greater quantity of commodities; and the people, as they can afford it, as they have more commodities to give for it, will naturally buy more and more plate. Their quantity of coin will rise out of necessity; their quantity of plate out of vanity and ostentation, or for the same reason that the quantity of fine statues, pictures, and every other luxury and curiosity is likely to rise among them. But just as sculptors and painters are not likely to be worse paid in times of wealth and prosperity than in times of poverty and depression, so gold and silver are not likely to be worse paid for.

The price of gold and silver, when the accidental discovery of more abundant mines does not keep it down, naturally rises with the wealth of every country; and so, whatever the state of the mines, it is at all times naturally higher in a rich country than in a poor one. Gold and silver, like all other commodities, naturally seek the market where the best price is given for them, and the best price is commonly given for everything in the country best able to afford it. Labour, it must be remembered, is the ultimate price paid for everything; and in countries where labour is equally well rewarded, the money price of labour will be in proportion to the money price of the labourer's subsistence. But gold and silver will naturally exchange for more subsistence in a rich country than in a poor one, in a country that abounds with subsistence than in one only poorly supplied with it. If the two countries are far apart, the difference may be very great; for though the metals naturally fly from the worse to the better market, it may be hard to carry them in such quantities as to bring their price nearly to a level in both. If the countries are near, the difference will be smaller, and may sometimes be barely perceptible, because in this case the transport will be easy. China is a much richer country than any part of Europe, and the difference between the price of subsistence in China and in Europe is very great. Rice in China is much cheaper than wheat is anywhere in Europe. England is a much richer country than Scotland, but the difference between the money price of corn in the two countries is much smaller, and barely perceptible. Measured by quantity, Scotch corn generally appears a good deal cheaper than English; but measured by quality, it is certainly somewhat dearer. Scotland receives very large supplies from England almost every year, and every commodity must usually be somewhat dearer in the country it is brought to than in the country it comes from. English corn, then, must be dearer in Scotland than in England; and yet, measured by its quality, or by the quantity and goodness of the flour or meal that can be made from it, it cannot commonly be sold higher there than the Scotch corn that comes to market in competition with it.

The difference between the money price of labour in China and in Europe is even greater than the difference between the money price of subsistence, because the real reward of labour is higher in Europe than in China, most of Europe being in an improving state while China seems to be standing still. The money price of labour is lower in Scotland than in England because the real reward of labour is much lower: Scotland, though advancing to greater wealth, advances much more slowly than England. The frequency of emigration from Scotland and its rarity from England prove well enough that the demand for labour is very different in the two countries. The proportion between the real reward of labour in different countries, it must be remembered, is naturally governed not by their actual wealth or poverty but by whether their condition is advancing, stationary, or declining.

Gold and silver, just as they are naturally of the greatest value among the richest nations, so they are naturally of the least value among the poorest. Among savages, the poorest of all nations, they are scarcely of any value.

In great towns, corn is always dearer than in remote parts of the country. This, however, is the effect not of the real cheapness of silver but of the real dearness of corn. It costs no less labour to bring silver to the great town than to the remote parts of the country; but it costs a great deal more to bring corn.

In some very rich and commercial countries, such as Holland and the territory of Genoa, corn is dear for the same reason that it is dear in great towns. They do not produce enough to feed their inhabitants. They are rich in the industry and skill of their craftsmen and manufacturers, in every sort of machinery that can ease and shorten labour, in shipping, and in all the other instruments and means of carriage and commerce; but they are poor in corn, which, having to be brought to them from distant countries, must pay for the carriage from those countries by an addition to its price. It costs no less labour to bring silver to Amsterdam than to Danzig; but it costs a great deal more to bring corn. The real cost of silver must be nearly the same in both places, but that of corn must be very different. Reduce the real wealth of either Holland or the territory of Genoa while the number of their inhabitants stays the same; reduce their power to supply themselves from distant countries; and the price of corn, instead of sinking with the fall in the quantity of their silver that must accompany this decline, whether as its cause or its effect, will rise to famine prices. When we are short of necessaries, we must give up all superfluities, whose value rises in times of wealth and prosperity and sinks in times of poverty and distress. It is otherwise with necessaries. Their real price, the quantity of labour they can buy or command, rises in times of poverty and distress, and sinks in times of wealth and prosperity, which are always times of great abundance, for otherwise they could not be times of wealth and prosperity. Corn is a necessary; silver is only a superfluity.

Whatever, then, may have been the rise in the quantity of the precious metals between the middle of the fourteenth and that of the sixteenth century arising from the growth of wealth and improvement, it could have had no tendency to lower their value, either in Great Britain or in any other part of Europe. So if those who have collected the prices of things in ancient times had, during this period, no reason to infer a fall in the value of silver from anything they observed about the prices of corn or other commodities, they had still less reason to infer it from any supposed growth of wealth and improvement.
Second Period. But however varied the opinions of the learned may have been about the course of the value of silver during the first period, they are unanimous about it during the second.

From about 1570 to about 1640, over a period of about seventy years, the variation in the proportion between the value of silver and that of corn took quite the opposite course. Silver sank in its real value, exchanging for a smaller quantity of labour than before, and corn rose in its nominal price: instead of being commonly sold for about two ounces of silver the quarter, or about ten shillings of our present money, it came to be sold for six and eight ounces of silver the quarter, or about thirty and forty shillings of our present money.

The discovery of the abundant mines of America seems to have been the sole cause of this fall in the value of silver relative to that of corn. It is accounted for in the same way by everybody, and there has never been any dispute about the fact or about its cause. Most of Europe was during this period advancing in industry and improvement, so the demand for silver must have been rising; but the increase in supply had, it seems, so far outrun that in demand that the value of the metal sank considerably. The discovery of the mines of America, it should be noted, does not seem to have had any very noticeable effect on the prices of things in England until after 1570, even though the mines of Potosi had been discovered more than twenty years before.

From 1595 to 1620 inclusive, the average price of the quarter of nine bushels of the best wheat at Windsor market appears, from the accounts of Eton College, to have been £2 1s 6d ⁹⁄₁₃. From this sum, ignoring the fraction and deducting a ninth, or 4s 7⅓d, the price of the quarter of eight bushels comes out at £1 16s 10⅔d. And from this sum, again ignoring the fraction and deducting a ninth, or 4s 1⅑d, for the difference between the price of the best wheat and that of the middle wheat, the price of the middle wheat comes out at about £1 12s 8d ⁸⁄₉, or about six ounces and one-third of an ounce of silver.

From 1621 to 1636 inclusive, the average price of the same measure of the best wheat at the same market appears, from the same accounts, to have been £2 10s; from which, making the same deductions as before, the average price of the quarter of eight bushels of middle wheat comes out at £1 19s 6d, or about seven ounces and two-thirds of an ounce of silver.

Third Period. Between 1630 and 1640, or about 1636, the effect of the discovery of the mines of America in lowering the value of silver seems to have been completed, and the value of the metal seems never to have sunk lower relative to corn than it was about that time. It seems to have risen somewhat over the present century, and had probably begun to do so even some time before the end of the last.

From 1637 to 1700 inclusive, the sixty-four last years of the last century, the average price of the quarter of nine bushels of the best wheat at Windsor market appears, from the same accounts, to have been £2 11s 0⅓d, which is only 1s 0⅓d dearer than it had been during the sixteen years before. But over these sixty-four years two events occurred which must have caused a far greater scarcity of corn than the course of the seasons would otherwise have brought about, and which therefore, without supposing any further fall in the value of silver, more than account for this very small rise in price.

The first of these events was the civil war, which, by discouraging tillage and interrupting commerce, must have raised the price of corn far above what the course of the seasons would otherwise have brought about. It must have had this effect, more or less, at all the different markets in the kingdom, but particularly at those near London, which must be supplied from the greatest distance. In 1648, accordingly, the price of the best wheat at Windsor market appears, from the same accounts, to have been £4 5s, and in 1649 to have been £4, the quarter of nine bushels. The excess of those two years above £2 10s (the average price of the sixteen years before 1637) is £3 5s, which, spread over the sixty-four last years of the last century, will alone very nearly account for that small rise in price which seems to have occurred in them. These, however, though the highest, are by no means the only high prices that seem to have been caused by the civil wars.

The second event was the bounty on the export of corn, granted in 1688. Many people have thought that the bounty, by encouraging tillage, may over a long course of years have produced greater abundance and so greater cheapness of corn in the home market than would otherwise have prevailed there. How far the bounty could produce this effect at any time I shall examine later; I shall only note here that between 1688 and 1700 it had not had time to produce any such effect. During this short period its only effect must have been to raise the price in the home market, by encouraging the export of each year's surplus and thereby preventing the abundance of one year from making up for the scarcity of another. The scarcity that prevailed in England from 1693 to 1699 inclusive, though no doubt chiefly due to bad seasons and therefore extending over a considerable part of Europe, must have been somewhat worsened by the bounty. In 1699, accordingly, the further export of corn was forbidden for nine months.

There was a third event in this same period which, though it could not cause any scarcity of corn, nor perhaps any rise in the real quantity of silver usually paid for it, must necessarily have caused some rise in the nominal sum. This event was the great debasement of the silver coin by clipping and wearing. This evil had begun in the reign of Charles II and had gone on steadily increasing until 1695, at which time, as we may learn from Mr Lowndes, the current silver coin was on average near twenty-five per cent below its standard value. But the nominal sum that makes up the market price of every commodity is necessarily governed not so much by the quantity of silver that, according to the standard, ought to be in it, as by the quantity that experience finds actually is in it. This nominal sum, then, is necessarily higher when the coin is much debased by clipping and wearing than when it is near its standard value.

Over the present century, the silver coin has at no time been further below its standard weight than it is now. But though much defaced, its value has been kept up by that of the gold coin for which it is exchanged. For though, before the recent recoinage, the gold coin too was a good deal defaced, it was less so than the silver. In 1695, by contrast, the value of the silver coin was not kept up by the gold coin, a guinea then commonly exchanging for thirty shillings of the worn and clipped silver. Before the recent recoinage of the gold, the price of silver bullion was seldom higher than five shillings and sevenpence an ounce, which is only fivepence above the mint price. But in 1695 the common price of silver bullion was six shillings and fivepence an ounce (Lowndes's Essay on the Silver Coin, p. 68), which is fifteen pence above the mint price. Even before the recent recoinage of the gold, then, the coin, gold and silver together, when compared with silver bullion, was reckoned no more than eight per cent below its standard value; whereas in 1695 it had been reckoned near twenty-five per cent below it. But at the start of the present century, that is, just after the great recoinage in King William's time, most of the current silver coin must have been still nearer its standard weight than it is now. Over the present century, too, there has been no great public calamity, such as a civil war, to discourage tillage or interrupt the country's internal commerce. And though the bounty in force through most of this century must always raise the price of corn somewhat higher than it would otherwise be in the actual state of tillage, yet, since over this century the bounty has had full time to produce all the good effects commonly credited to it, namely to encourage tillage and so increase the quantity of corn in the home market, it may, on the principles of a system I shall explain and examine later, be supposed to have done something to lower the price of that commodity one way as well as to raise it the other. Many people suppose it has done more. In the sixty-four years of the present century, accordingly, the average price of the quarter of nine bushels of the best wheat at Windsor market appears, by the accounts of Eton College, to have been £2 0s 6d ¹⁰⁄₃₂, which is about ten shillings and sixpence, or more than twenty-five per cent, cheaper than during the sixty-four last years of the last century; about nine shillings and sixpence cheaper than during the sixteen years before 1636, when the discovery of the abundant mines of America may be supposed to have had its full effect; and about one shilling cheaper than in the twenty-six years before 1620, before that discovery can well be supposed to have had its full effect. By this account, the average price of middle wheat during these sixty-four first years of the present century comes out at about thirty-two shillings the quarter of eight bushels.
The value of silver, then, seems to have risen somewhat relative to that of corn over the course of the present century, and had probably begun to do so even some time before the end of the last.
In 1687 a quarter of nine bushels of the best wheat sold at Windsor market for £1:5:2. That was the lowest price it had reached since 1595.

In 1688 Gregory King, a man famous for his expertise in these matters, estimated that in years of moderate plenty the average price of wheat came to 3s. 6d. a bushel for the grower, or twenty-eight shillings a quarter. By the grower's price I take him to mean what is sometimes called the contract price—the price at which a farmer agrees, for a fixed number of years, to deliver a set quantity of corn to a dealer. Because a contract of this kind spares the farmer the cost and trouble of going to market, the contract price is generally lower than the supposed average market price. King reckoned twenty-eight shillings a quarter to be the usual contract price at that time in years of moderate plenty. Before the scarcity caused by the recent run of unusually bad seasons, I have been assured, it was the usual contract price in all ordinary years.

In 1688 Parliament granted the bounty on the export of corn. The country gentlemen, who then made up an even larger share of the legislature than they do now, had noticed that the money price of corn was falling. The bounty was a device meant to push it back up artificially to the high level at which it had often sold in the reigns of Charles I and II. It was therefore to remain in force until wheat reached forty-eight shillings a quarter—twenty shillings, or five-sevenths, dearer than the grower's price that King had estimated in that very year for times of moderate plenty. If his calculations deserve any of the wide reputation they have earned, forty-eight shillings a quarter was a price that, without some such device as the bounty, could not have been expected at that time except in years of extraordinary scarcity. But King William's government was not yet firmly established. It was in no position to refuse anything to the country gentlemen, from whom it was at that very moment seeking the first grant of the annual land-tax.

The value of silver, then, measured against that of corn, had probably risen somewhat before the end of the last century, and it seems to have gone on rising through most of the present one—though the bounty, by its inevitable workings, must have kept that rise from being as noticeable as it otherwise would have been given the actual state of farming.

In plentiful years the bounty causes an unusually large export, and this necessarily raises the price of corn above what it would otherwise be in such years. Encouraging tillage by keeping the price of corn up, even in the most plentiful years, was the openly stated aim of the policy.

In years of severe scarcity, it is true, the bounty has generally been suspended. Even so, it must have had some effect on the prices of many of those years. By the heavy export it causes in years of plenty, it must often prevent the surplus of one year from making up for the shortfall of another.

In years of plenty and in years of scarcity alike, then, the bounty pushes the price of corn above its natural level for the actual state of farming. So if the average price during the first sixty-four years of the present century has been lower than during the last sixty-four years of the previous one, then, with the same state of farming, the difference would have been far greater still without this workings of the bounty.

It may be objected that, without the bounty, the state of farming would not have been the same. I shall try to explain later what effects this policy may have had on the country's agriculture, when I come to deal specifically with bounties. For now I will only note that this rise in the value of silver relative to corn has not been peculiar to England. Three very reliable, careful, and hard-working compilers of corn prices—Dupré de St Maur, Messance, and the author of the Essay on the Police of Grain—have observed the same rise in France over the same period, and in nearly the same proportion. But in France, until 1764, the export of grain was banned by law; and it is rather hard to suppose that nearly the same fall in price which occurred in one country despite this ban should, in another, be due to the extraordinary encouragement given to export.

It would perhaps be more accurate to regard this change in the average money price of corn as the result of some gradual rise in the real value of silver in the European market, rather than of any fall in the real average value of corn. Corn, as already noted, is over long stretches of time a more accurate measure of value than silver or perhaps any other commodity. When, after the discovery of America's rich mines, corn rose to three and four times its former money price, everyone ascribed the change not to any rise in the real value of corn but to a fall in the real value of silver. By the same logic, then, if the average money price of corn during the first sixty-four years of this century has fallen somewhat below its level during most of the last, we should attribute the change not to any fall in the real value of corn but to some rise in the real value of silver in the European market.

The high price of corn over these last ten or twelve years has, admittedly, raised a suspicion that the real value of silver in the European market is still falling. Yet this high price clearly seems to have been caused by the extraordinary badness of the seasons, and should therefore be treated not as permanent but as a passing, occasional event. For these ten or twelve years the seasons have been unfavourable across most of Europe, and the disorders in Poland have greatly worsened the scarcity in all those countries that, in dear years, used to draw supplies from that market. So long a run of bad seasons, though not very common, is by no means unique; anyone who has looked closely into the history of corn prices in earlier times will easily recall several other examples of the same kind. Ten years of extraordinary scarcity, moreover, are no more remarkable than ten years of extraordinary plenty. The low price of corn from 1741 to 1750 inclusive may fairly be set against its high price during these last eight or ten years. From 1741 to 1750, according to the accounts of Eton College, the average price of a quarter of nine bushels of the best wheat at Windsor market was only £1:13:9⅞, which is nearly 6s. 3d. below the average price of the first sixty-four years of this century. By this same account the average price of a quarter of eight bushels of middling wheat works out, over those ten years, at only £1:6:8.

Between 1741 and 1750, however, the bounty must have kept the price of corn in the home market from falling as low as it naturally would have. The custom-house books show that during these ten years the quantity of grain of all sorts exported came to no less than 8,029,156 quarters and one bushel. The bounty paid on this amounted to £1,514,962:17:4½. Accordingly, in 1749 Mr Pelham, then prime minister, pointed out to the House of Commons that, over the three preceding years, an extraordinary sum had been paid as bounty for exporting corn. He had good reason to say so, and the following year he could have said it with even more force: in that single year the bounty paid came to no less than £324,176:10:6 (see Tracts on the Corn Trade, Tract 3). There is no need to spell out how much this forced export must have raised the price of corn in the home market above what it otherwise would have been.

At the end of the accounts attached to this chapter the reader will find a separate breakdown of those ten years. He will also find there a separate breakdown of the preceding ten years, whose average is likewise below—though not so far below—the general average of the first sixty-four years of the century. The year 1740, however, was a year of extraordinary scarcity. These twenty years before 1750 may fairly be set against the twenty before 1770. Just as the earlier twenty fell well below the general average of the century, despite one or two dear years in between, so the later twenty have run well above it, despite one or two cheap years in between, such as 1759. If the earlier period has not fallen as far below the general average as the later one has risen above it, we should probably credit the difference to the bounty. The change has plainly been too sudden to be put down to any change in the value of silver, which is always slow and gradual. The suddenness of the effect can only be explained by a cause that can act suddenly—the accidental variations of the seasons.

The money price of labour in Great Britain has indeed risen over the course of this century. Yet this seems to result not so much from any fall in the value of silver in the European market as from an increase in the demand for labour in Great Britain, arising from the great and almost universal prosperity of the country. In France, a country not quite so prosperous, the money price of labour has been observed, since the middle of the last century, to sink gradually along with the average money price of corn. Both in the last century and in this one, the daily wages of common labour there are said to have run pretty uniformly at about a twentieth of the average price of the septier of wheat—a measure holding a little more than four Winchester bushels. In Great Britain, as already shown, the real reward of labour—the actual quantity of necessaries and comforts given to the labourer—has increased considerably over this century. The rise in its money price seems to have resulted not from any fall in the value of silver in the general market of Europe, but from a rise in the real price of labour in the particular market of Great Britain, owing to the peculiarly fortunate circumstances of the country.

For some time after America was first discovered, silver went on selling at its former price, or not much below it. The profits of mining were for a while very great and well above their natural rate. But those who brought the metal into Europe soon found that the whole annual import could not be sold off at this high price. Silver gradually exchanged for smaller and smaller quantities of goods. Its price sank lower and lower until it reached its natural price—the level just sufficient to pay, at their natural rates, the wages of labour, the profits of stock, and the rent of land needed to bring it from the mine to market. In most of the silver mines of Peru, as already noted, the king of Spain's tax—a tenth of the gross produce—swallows the whole rent of the land. This tax was originally a half; it soon dropped to a third, then to a fifth, and at last to a tenth, where it still stands. In most of Peru's silver mines this tenth, it seems, is all that is left after replacing the operator's stock together with its ordinary profits; and it is generally agreed that these profits, once very high, are now as low as they can be while still allowing the works to be carried on.

The king of Spain's tax was cut to a fifth of the registered silver in 1504 (Solorzano, vol. ii), forty-one years before 1545, the date the mines of Potosi were discovered. In the ninety years that followed, before 1636, these mines—the most fertile in all America—had time enough to produce their full effect, that is, to drive the value of silver in the European market as low as it could well fall while still paying this tax to the king of Spain. Ninety years is enough time to bring any commodity that is not under monopoly down to its natural price, or to the lowest price at which, while paying a particular tax, it can keep selling for any considerable stretch of time.

The price of silver in the European market might perhaps have fallen still lower, and it might have become necessary either to cut the tax on it not just to one-tenth, as in 1736, but to one-twentieth, as was done with gold, or else to abandon working most of the American mines now in operation. The gradual rise in the demand for silver—the gradual widening of the market for the produce of America's silver mines—is probably what has prevented this. It has not only kept up the value of silver in the European market but has perhaps even raised it somewhat above what it was around the middle of the last century.
Since America was first discovered, the market for the produce of its silver mines has been growing steadily larger.

First, the European market has grown steadily larger. Since the discovery of America, most of Europe has greatly improved. England, Holland, France, and Germany—and even Sweden, Denmark, and Russia—have all advanced considerably in both agriculture and manufactures. Italy seems not to have gone backwards. Italy's decline came before the conquest of Peru; since then it seems rather to have recovered a little. Spain and Portugal, it is true, are supposed to have gone backwards. But Portugal is only a very small part of Europe, and Spain's decline is perhaps not as great as is commonly imagined. At the start of the sixteenth century Spain was a very poor country, even compared with France, which has improved so much since. The emperor Charles V, who had travelled so often through both countries, famously remarked that everything was abundant in France but everything was lacking in Spain. The growing output of Europe's agriculture and manufactures must necessarily have called for a gradual increase in the quantity of silver coin to circulate it, and the growing number of wealthy individuals must have called for a similar increase in the quantity of their plate and other silver ornaments.

Secondly, America is itself a new market for the produce of its own silver mines; and since its advances in agriculture, industry, and population are far more rapid than those of the most thriving countries in Europe, its demand must grow far faster too. The English colonies are altogether a new market, which, partly for coin and partly for plate, calls for a continually growing supply of silver across a great continent where there had never before been any demand. Most of the Spanish and Portuguese colonies are likewise entirely new markets. New Granada, Yucatan, Paraguay, and Brazil, before the Europeans discovered them, were inhabited by savage nations that had neither arts nor agriculture. A considerable amount of both has now been introduced into all of them. Even Mexico and Peru, though not wholly new markets, are certainly far larger ones than they ever were before. After all the wonderful tales published about the splendid state of those countries in ancient times, anyone who reads the history of their first discovery and conquest with any sober judgment will plainly see that, in arts, agriculture, and commerce, their inhabitants were far more ignorant than the Tartars of the Ukraine are today. Even the Peruvians, the more civilized of the two nations, though they used gold and silver as ornaments, had no coined money of any kind. Their whole commerce was carried on by barter, and so there was scarcely any division of labour among them. Those who tilled the ground had to build their own houses, make their own furniture, and make their own clothes, shoes, and farm implements. The few craftsmen among them are said to have all been kept by the sovereign, the nobles, and the priests, and were probably their servants or slaves. None of the ancient arts of Mexico and Peru has ever supplied Europe with a single manufacture. The Spanish armies, though they scarcely ever exceeded five hundred men and often were not half that number, met almost everywhere with great difficulty in finding food. The famines they are said to have caused almost wherever they went—in countries that are at the same time described as very populous and well cultivated—are proof enough that the story of this populousness and high cultivation is largely a fable. The Spanish colonies are under a government in many respects less favourable to agriculture, improvement, and population than that of the English colonies. Even so, they seem to be advancing in all these far more rapidly than any country in Europe. In a fertile soil and a pleasant climate, the great abundance and cheapness of land—something common to all new colonies—is, it seems, so great an advantage that it makes up for many defects in civil government. Frezier, who visited Peru in 1713, describes Lima as containing between twenty-five and twenty-eight thousand inhabitants. Ulloa, who lived in the same country between 1740 and 1746, describes it as containing more than fifty thousand. The difference in their accounts of the populations of several other principal towns of Chile and Peru is nearly the same; and since there seems no reason to doubt the good information of either, this marks a rate of growth scarcely below that of the English colonies. America, then, is a new market for the produce of its own silver mines, and its demand must grow far faster than that of the most thriving country in Europe.

Thirdly, the East Indies is another market for the produce of America's silver mines, and one that, ever since those mines were first discovered, has been steadily absorbing greater and greater quantities of silver. Since that time the direct trade between America and the East Indies, carried on by the Acapulco ships, has been continually growing, and the indirect trade by way of Europe has grown in an even greater proportion. During the sixteenth century the Portuguese were the only European nation carrying on any regular trade to the East Indies. In the closing years of that century the Dutch began to encroach on this monopoly, and within a few years drove them out of their chief settlements in India. Through most of the last century those two nations divided the bulk of the East India trade between them, the Dutch trade continually growing in an even greater proportion than the Portuguese declined. The English and French carried on some trade with India in the last century, but it has grown greatly in this one. The East India trade of the Swedes and the Danes began during this century. Even the Muscovites now trade regularly with China, by a kind of caravan that travels overland through Siberia and Tartary to Pekin. The East India trade of all these nations—except that of the French, which the last war had all but destroyed—has been almost continually growing. The rising consumption of East India goods in Europe is, it seems, so great as to give a gradual increase of employment to all of them. Tea, for example, was a substance very little used in Europe before the middle of the last century. At present the value of the tea imported each year by the English East India Company for the use of their own countrymen comes to more than a million and a half a year; and even this is not enough, since a great deal more is constantly smuggled into the country from the ports of Holland, from Gottenburgh in Sweden, and from the coast of France too, as long as the French East India Company was thriving. The consumption of China's porcelain, of the spices of the Moluccas, of the piece goods of Bengal, and of countless other articles has grown in very nearly the same proportion. Accordingly, the total tonnage of all European shipping employed in the East India trade at any one time during the last century was perhaps not much greater than that of the English East India Company alone before its recent reduction of shipping.

But in the East Indies—particularly in China and Hindustan—the value of the precious metals, when the Europeans first began trading there, was much higher than in Europe, and it still is. In rice countries, which generally yield two and sometimes three crops a year, each more plentiful than any ordinary corn crop, the abundance of food must be far greater than in any corn country of equal size. Such countries are accordingly far more populous. There, too, the rich, having a much greater surplus of food to dispose of beyond what they themselves can consume, have the means to buy a far greater quantity of other people's labour. The retinue of a grandee in China or Hindustan is accordingly, by all accounts, far more numerous and splendid than that of the richest subjects in Europe. The same surplus of food at their disposal enables them to give a greater quantity of it for all those rare and unusual things that nature furnishes only in very small amounts, such as the precious metals and precious stones, the great objects of competition among the rich. Even if the mines that supplied the Indian market had been as rich as those that supplied the European, such goods would naturally have exchanged for a greater quantity of food in India than in Europe. But the mines supplying India with precious metals seem to have been a good deal less abundant, and those supplying it with precious stones a good deal more abundant, than the mines that supplied Europe. The precious metals, then, would naturally exchange in India for a somewhat greater quantity of precious stones, and for a much greater quantity of food, than in Europe. The money price of diamonds, the greatest of all luxuries, would be somewhat lower, and that of food, the first of all necessaries, a great deal lower, in the one country than in the other. But the real price of labour—the actual quantity of necessaries given to the labourer—is, as already noted, lower in both China and Hindustan, the two great markets of India, than throughout most of Europe. The labourer's wages will buy a smaller quantity of food there; and since the money price of food is much lower in India than in Europe, the money price of labour is lower there on two counts at once—on account both of the small quantity of food it will buy and of the low price of that food. But in countries of equal skill and industry, the money price of most manufactures will be in proportion to the money price of labour; and in manufacturing skill and industry China and Hindustan, though inferior, seem not much inferior to any part of Europe. The money price of most manufactures will therefore naturally be much lower in those great empires than anywhere in Europe. Across most of Europe, moreover, the cost of land carriage greatly raises both the real and the nominal price of most manufactures. It takes more labour, and therefore more money, to bring first the raw materials and then the finished goods to market. In China and Hindustan the extent and variety of inland waterways spare most of this labour, and so most of this money, and thereby push down still further both the real and the nominal price of most of their manufactures. For all these reasons the precious metals are a commodity that always has been, and still is, extremely advantageous to carry from Europe to India. There is scarcely any commodity that fetches a better price there, or that, in proportion to the quantity of labour and goods it costs in Europe, will buy or command a greater quantity of labour and goods in India. It is also more advantageous to carry silver there than gold, because in China and most of the other markets of India the proportion between fine silver and fine gold is only about ten, or at most twelve, to one, whereas in Europe it is fourteen or fifteen to one. In China and most of the other markets of India, ten or at most twelve ounces of silver will buy an ounce of gold; in Europe it takes from fourteen to fifteen ounces. In the cargoes of most European ships sailing to India, therefore, silver has generally been one of the most valuable items. It is the most valuable item in the Acapulco ships that sail to Manilla. The silver of the new continent seems in this way to be one of the chief goods by which the trade between the two ends of the old one is carried on; and it is largely by means of it that those distant parts of the world are linked together.

To supply so vastly extended a market, the quantity of silver brought from the mines each year must be enough not only to sustain the continual increase, in both coin and plate, that every thriving country requires, but also to make good the continual wear and consumption of silver that occurs in every country where the metal is used.

The continual loss of the precious metals—of coin by wear, and of plate by both wear and cleaning—is very noticeable, and in goods so widely used it would by itself call for a very large annual supply. The consumption of these metals in certain manufactures, though it may not on the whole be greater than this gradual wastage, is far more noticeable because it is far more rapid. In the manufactures of Birmingham alone, the quantity of gold and silver used each year in gilding and plating, and thereby permanently kept from ever again appearing in metallic form, is said to amount to more than fifty thousand pounds sterling. From this we may form some idea of how great the annual consumption must be across all the different parts of the world, whether in manufactures like those of Birmingham or in laces, embroideries, gold and silver cloth, the gilding of books, furniture, and so on. A considerable quantity, too, must be lost every year in transporting these metals from place to place, both by sea and by land. In most of the governments of Asia, moreover, the almost universal habit of burying treasure in the ground—whose whereabouts often die with the person who hid it—must cause the loss of a still greater quantity.

The quantity of gold and silver imported at both Cadiz and Lisbon—including not only what is registered but also what is presumed to be smuggled—comes, by the best accounts, to about six million sterling a year.

According to Mr Meggens (Postscript to the Universal Merchant, pp. 15 and 16—this postscript was not printed until 1756, three years after the book itself, which has never had a second edition, so the postscript is found in few copies; it corrects several errors in the book), the annual import of precious metals into Spain, averaged over six years from 1748 to 1753 inclusive, and into Portugal, averaged over seven years from 1747 to 1753 inclusive, came to 1,101,107 pounds weight of silver and 49,940 pounds weight of gold. The silver, at sixty-two shillings the pound troy, amounts to £3,413,431:10s. sterling. The gold, at forty-four guineas and a half the pound troy, amounts to £2,333,446:14s. sterling. Together they come to £5,746,878:4s. sterling. The account of what was imported under register, he assures us, is exact. He gives the details of the particular places the gold and silver came from, and of the particular quantity of each metal that, according to the register, each of them supplied. He also makes an allowance for the quantity of each metal that he supposes may have been smuggled. The great experience of this judicious merchant gives his opinion considerable weight.

According to the eloquent, and sometimes well-informed, author of the Philosophical and Political History of the Establishment of the Europeans in the two Indies, the annual import of registered gold and silver into Spain, averaged over eleven years from 1754 to 1764 inclusive, came to 13,984,185⅗ piastres of ten reals. Allowing for what may have been smuggled, however, he supposes the whole annual import may have come to seventeen million piastres, which at 4s. 6d. the piastre equals £3,825,000 sterling. He gives the details, too, of the particular places the gold and silver came from, and of the particular quantities of each metal that, according to the register, each of them supplied. He also tells us that if we were to judge the quantity of gold imported each year from Brazil to Lisbon by the amount of tax paid to the king of Portugal—which, it seems, is one-fifth of the standard metal—we might value it at eighteen million cruzadoes, or forty-five million French livres, equal to about twenty million sterling. Allowing for what may have been smuggled, however, he says we may safely add an eighth more, or £250,000 sterling, so that the whole comes to £2,250,000 sterling. By this account, then, the whole annual import of precious metals into both Spain and Portugal comes to about £6,075,000 sterling.

Several other very well-authenticated, though manuscript, accounts, I have been assured, agree in putting this whole annual import, on average, at about six million sterling, sometimes a little more, sometimes a little less.

The annual import of precious metals into Cadiz and Lisbon is not, however, equal to the whole annual produce of America's mines. Some part is sent each year by the Acapulco ships to Manilla; some part is used in a contraband trade that the Spanish colonies carry on with those of other European nations; and some part, no doubt, stays in the country. America's mines, besides, are by no means the only gold and silver mines in the world. They are, however, by far the most abundant. The produce of all the other known mines is admittedly trifling compared with theirs, and the far greater part of their produce, it is also admitted, is imported each year into Cadiz and Lisbon. But the consumption of Birmingham alone, at fifty thousand pounds a year, equals a hundred-and-twentieth part of this annual import of six million a year. The whole annual consumption of gold and silver, then, across all the different countries of the world where these metals are used, may perhaps be nearly equal to the whole annual produce. The remainder may be no more than enough to meet the growing demand of all thriving countries. It may even have fallen so far short of this demand as to raise somewhat the price of these metals in the European market.

The quantity of brass and iron brought from the mine to market each year is out of all proportion greater than that of gold and silver. Yet on this account we do not imagine that these coarse metals are likely to multiply beyond demand or to grow steadily cheaper. Why, then, should we imagine that the precious metals are likely to do so? The coarse metals, though harder, are put to much harder uses, and, being less valuable, are less carefully preserved. The precious metals, however, are no more immortal than they; they too are liable to be lost, wasted, and used up in a great variety of ways.

The price of all metals, though subject to slow and gradual variations, varies less from year to year than that of almost any other part of the raw produce of land; and the price of the precious metals is even less subject to sudden swings than that of the coarse ones. The durability of metals is the foundation of this remarkable steadiness of price. The corn brought to market last year will all, or almost all, be consumed long before the end of this year. But some of the iron brought from the mine two or three hundred years ago may still be in use, and perhaps some of the gold brought from it two or three thousand years ago. The different masses of corn that, in different years, must supply the world's consumption will always be roughly in proportion to the respective produce of those years. But the proportion between the masses of iron in use in two different years will be very little affected by any accidental difference in the output of the iron mines in those two years; and the proportion between the masses of gold will be affected still less by any such difference in the output of the gold mines. So although the produce of most metallic mines varies perhaps even more from year to year than that of most cornfields, those variations do not affect the price of the one kind of commodity as they do that of the other.
Variations in the Proportion between the Respective Values of Gold and Silver.

Before the discovery of America's mines, the value of fine gold to fine silver was fixed in the various mints of Europe at somewhere between one to ten and one to twelve; that is, an ounce of fine gold was reckoned worth from ten to twelve ounces of fine silver. About the middle of the last century it came to be fixed at between one to fourteen and one to fifteen; that is, an ounce of fine gold came to be reckoned worth between fourteen and fifteen ounces of fine silver. Gold rose in its nominal value, or in the quantity of silver given for it. Both metals fell in their real value, or in the quantity of labour they could buy; but silver fell more than gold. Though both the gold and silver mines of America surpassed in richness all those ever known before, the richness of the silver mines had, it seems, been proportionally still greater than that of the gold.

The great quantities of silver carried each year from Europe to India have, in some of the English settlements, gradually lowered the value of that metal relative to gold. In the mint of Calcutta, an ounce of fine gold is reckoned worth fifteen ounces of fine silver, just as in Europe. There it is perhaps rated too high in the mint for the value it bears in the market of Bengal. In China the proportion of gold to silver still stands at one to ten, or one to twelve. In Japan it is said to be one to eight.

The proportion between the quantities of gold and silver imported each year into Europe is, according to Mr Meggens' account, nearly one to twenty-two; that is, for every ounce of gold a little more than twenty-two ounces of silver are imported. The great quantity of silver sent each year to the East Indies reduces, he supposes, the quantities of the two metals that remain in Europe to the proportion of one to fourteen or fifteen—the proportion of their values. He seems to think the proportion between their values must necessarily be the same as that between their quantities, and would therefore be one to twenty-two, were it not for this heavier export of silver.

But the usual proportion between the values of two commodities is not necessarily the same as the proportion between the quantities of them commonly on the market. The price of an ox, reckoned at ten guineas, is about sixty times the price of a lamb, reckoned at 3s. 6d. Yet it would be absurd to conclude from this that there are usually sixty lambs on the market for every ox; and it is just as absurd to conclude, because an ounce of gold will usually buy fourteen or fifteen ounces of silver, that there are usually only fourteen or fifteen ounces of silver on the market for every ounce of gold.

The quantity of silver usually on the market is probably much greater in proportion to that of gold than the value of a given quantity of gold is to that of an equal quantity of silver. The whole quantity of a cheap commodity brought to market is commonly not only greater but of greater total value than the whole quantity of a dear one. The whole quantity of bread brought to market each year is not only greater but of greater value than the whole quantity of butcher's meat; the whole quantity of butcher's meat than the whole quantity of poultry; and the whole quantity of poultry than the whole quantity of wild fowl. There are so many more buyers for the cheap commodity than for the dear one that not only a greater quantity but a greater total value of it can usually be sold. The whole quantity of the cheap commodity must therefore commonly be greater, in proportion to the whole quantity of the dear one, than the value of a given quantity of the dear one is to the value of an equal quantity of the cheap one. When we compare the precious metals with each other, silver is the cheap commodity and gold the dear one. We should naturally expect, then, that there is always on the market not only a greater quantity but a greater total value of silver than of gold. Let anyone who has a little of both compare his silver plate with his gold plate, and he will probably find that not only the quantity but the value of the former greatly exceeds that of the latter. Many people, besides, have a good deal of silver but no gold plate, which even among those who own it is generally limited to watch-cases, snuff-boxes, and such trinkets, whose total value is seldom great. In the British coinage, it is true, the value of the gold greatly outweighs the silver, but this is not so in the coinage of every country. In some countries the value of the two metals in coin is nearly equal. In the Scottish coinage, before the union with England, the gold outweighed the silver very little, though it did so somewhat (see Ruddiman's Preface to Anderson's Diplomata, etc. Scotiae), as appears from the mint accounts. In the coinage of many countries the silver outweighs the gold. In France the largest sums are commonly paid in silver, and it is hard there to get more gold than what is needed to carry about in your pocket. But the greater value of silver plate over gold, which holds in every country, will far more than make up for the greater weight of gold in the coinage, which holds only in some.

Though in one sense silver always has been, and probably always will be, much cheaper than gold, yet in another sense gold may perhaps, in the present state of the Spanish market, be said to be somewhat cheaper than silver. A commodity may be called dear or cheap not only by the absolute size of its usual price but by how far that price stands above the lowest at which it can be brought to market for any considerable time together. This lowest price is the one that barely replaces, with a moderate profit, the stock that must be used to bring the commodity there. It is the price that yields nothing to the landlord, of which rent forms no part, and which resolves itself wholly into wages and profit. Now in the present state of the Spanish market, gold certainly stands somewhat nearer to this lowest price than silver. The king of Spain's tax on gold is only one-twentieth of the standard metal, or five per cent, whereas his tax on silver comes to one-tenth, or ten per cent. In these taxes, as already noted, consists the whole rent of most of the gold and silver mines of Spanish America; and the tax on gold is even worse paid than that on silver. The profits of the operators of gold mines, too, since they more rarely make a fortune, must in general be even more moderate than those of the operators of silver mines. The price of Spanish gold, then, yielding both less rent and less profit, must in the Spanish market stand somewhat nearer to the lowest price for which it can be brought there than the price of Spanish silver. When all costs are reckoned, the whole quantity of the one metal cannot, it seems, be sold off in the Spanish market as advantageously as the whole quantity of the other. The king of Portugal's tax on the gold of Brazil is, it is true, the same as the old tax of the king of Spain on the silver of Mexico and Peru—one-fifth of the standard metal. It may therefore be uncertain whether, to the general market of Europe, the whole mass of American gold arrives at a price nearer to the lowest for which it can be brought there than the whole mass of American silver.
The price of diamonds and other precious stones may perhaps stand still nearer to the lowest price at which they can be brought to market than even the price of gold.

It is not very likely that any part of a tax that is laid on one of the most suitable subjects of taxation—a mere luxury and superfluity—and that yields so important a revenue as the tax on silver, will ever be given up so long as it can possibly be paid. Yet the same impossibility of paying it, which in 1736 made it necessary to cut it from one-fifth to one-tenth, may in time make it necessary to cut it still further, just as it made it necessary to reduce the tax on gold to one-twentieth. That the silver mines of Spanish America, like all other mines, grow gradually more expensive to work—on account of the greater depths at which the works must be carried on, and the greater expense of draining out the water and supplying fresh air at those depths—is acknowledged by everyone who has looked into the state of those mines.

These causes, which amount to a growing scarcity of silver (a commodity may be said to grow scarcer when it becomes harder and more expensive to gather a given quantity of it), must in time produce one of three results. The increased expense must either, first, be offset entirely by a proportional rise in the price of the metal; or, secondly, be offset entirely by a proportional cut in the tax on silver; or, thirdly, be offset partly by the one and partly by the other. This third result is quite possible. Just as gold rose in price relative to silver despite a great cut in the tax on gold, so silver might rise in price relative to labour and goods despite an equal cut in the tax on silver.

Such successive cuts in the tax, however, though they may not prevent the rise in the value of silver in the European market altogether, must certainly slow it more or less. As a result of such cuts, many mines may be worked that could not be worked before because they could not afford to pay the old tax; and so the quantity of silver brought to market each year must always be somewhat greater, and therefore the value of any given quantity somewhat less, than it otherwise would have been. As a result of the cut in 1736, the value of silver in the European market, though it may not today be lower than before that cut, is probably at least ten per cent lower than it would have been had the court of Spain gone on exacting the old tax. That, despite this cut, the value of silver has during this century begun to rise somewhat in the European market is something the facts and arguments set out above incline me to believe—or, more properly, to suspect and conjecture; for the best opinion I can form on this subject scarcely deserves the name of belief. The rise, supposing there has been any, has so far been so very small that, after all that has been said, it may still seem doubtful to many people not only whether it has actually happened, but whether the opposite may not have happened, or whether the value of silver may not still be falling in the European market.

It must be noted, however, that whatever the supposed annual import of gold and silver may be, there must come a point at which the annual consumption of these metals equals that annual import. Their consumption must grow as their mass grows—indeed in a much greater proportion. As their mass grows, their value falls. They are used more and cared for less, and so their consumption grows in a greater proportion than their mass. After a certain point, then, the annual consumption of these metals must in this way become equal to their annual import, provided that import is not continually increasing—which, in present times, is not thought to be the case.

If, once the annual consumption has come to equal the annual import, the annual import should gradually fall off, the annual consumption may for a time exceed the annual import. The mass of these metals may gradually and imperceptibly shrink, and their value gradually and imperceptibly rise, until the annual import becomes steady again and the annual consumption gradually and imperceptibly adjusts itself to what that import can sustain.
Grounds of the Suspicion that the Value of Silver still continues to decrease.

The increase of Europe's wealth, together with the popular notion that, since the quantity of precious metals naturally grows with wealth, their value falls as their quantity grows, may incline many people to believe that their value is still falling in the European market; and the still gradually rising price of many parts of the raw produce of land may confirm them further in this view.

I have already tried to show that the increase in the quantity of precious metals which arises in any country from an increase of wealth has no tendency to lower their value. Gold and silver naturally flow to a rich country for the same reason that all sorts of luxuries and curiosities flow to it: not because they are cheaper there than in poorer countries, but because they are dearer, or because a better price is given for them. It is the higher price that draws them; and as soon as that advantage ceases, they necessarily cease to go there.

I have already tried to show that, leaving aside corn and other vegetables raised entirely by human industry, all other kinds of raw produce—cattle, poultry, game of every kind, the useful fossils and minerals of the earth, and so on—naturally grow dearer as society advances in wealth and improvement. So even though such goods come to exchange for a greater quantity of silver than before, it does not follow that silver has become really cheaper, or will buy less labour than before; rather, those goods have become really dearer, and will buy more labour than before. It is not only their nominal price but their real price that rises as improvement advances. The rise in their nominal price results not from any debasement in the value of silver but from the rise in their real price.
Different Effects of the Progress of Improvement upon three different sorts of raw Produce.

These different kinds of raw produce may be divided into three classes. The first takes in those which human industry is scarcely able to multiply at all. The second, those it can multiply in proportion to demand. The third, those in which the power of industry is either limited or uncertain. As wealth and improvement advance, the real price of the first may rise to any degree of extravagance, and seems bound by no fixed limit. That of the second, though it may rise greatly, has a fixed limit beyond which it cannot well pass for any considerable time.
