That of the third, though its natural tendency is to rise as improvement advances, may yet at the same stage of improvement sometimes even fall, sometimes stay the same, and sometimes rise more or less, according as different accidents make human industry more or less successful in multiplying this kind of raw produce.

First Sort. The first kind of raw produce whose price rises as improvement advances is that which human industry is scarcely able to multiply at all. It consists of the things nature produces only in fixed quantities, and which, being highly perishable, cannot have the produce of many different seasons accumulated together. Such are most rare and unusual birds and fish, many kinds of game, almost all wild fowl, birds of passage in particular, and many other things. As wealth and the luxury that goes with it increase, the demand for these is likely to increase with them, and no effort of human industry may be able to raise the supply much beyond what it was before this rise in demand. The quantity of such goods staying the same, or nearly so, while the competition to buy them steadily grows, their price may rise to any degree of extravagance, and seems bound by no fixed limit. If woodcocks should become so fashionable as to sell for twenty guineas apiece, no effort of human industry could raise the number brought to market much above what it is at present. The high prices the Romans paid, at the height of their grandeur, for rare birds and fish are easily explained in this way. Those prices were the effect not of the low value of silver in those times but of the high value of such rarities and curiosities as human industry could not multiply at will. The real value of silver was higher at Rome, for some time before and after the fall of the republic, than it is throughout most of Europe today. Three sestertii, equal to about sixpence sterling, was the price the republic paid for the modius or peck of the tithe wheat of Sicily. This price, however, was probably below the average market price, since the obligation to deliver their wheat at this rate was regarded as a tax on the Sicilian farmers. So when the Romans needed to order more corn than the tithe of wheat amounted to, they were bound by agreement to pay four sestertii, or eightpence sterling the peck, for the surplus; and this had probably been reckoned the moderate and reasonable—that is, the ordinary or average contract—price of those times. It equals about twenty-one shillings the quarter. Twenty-eight shillings the quarter was, before the recent years of scarcity, the ordinary contract price of English wheat, which is inferior in quality to the Sicilian and generally sells for a lower price in the European market. The value of silver in those ancient times, then, must have stood to its value at present as three to four inversely; that is, three ounces of silver would then have bought the same quantity of labour and goods that four ounces will buy today. So when we read in Pliny that Seius (Lib. X, c. 29) bought a white nightingale as a present for the empress Agrippina at the price of six thousand sestertii, equal to about fifty pounds of our present money, and that Asinius Celer (Lib. IX, c. 17) bought a surmullet at the price of eight thousand sestertii, equal to about sixty-six pounds thirteen shillings and fourpence of our present money, the extravagance of those prices, however much it may astonish us, is nevertheless apt to appear to us about a third less than it really was. Their real price—the quantity of labour and subsistence given away for them—was about a third more than their nominal price tends to convey to us today. For the nightingale Seius gave the command over a quantity of labour and subsistence equal to what £66:13:4 would buy today, and for the surmullet Asinius Celer gave command over a quantity equal to what £88:17:9 would buy. What caused the extravagance of those high prices was not so much the abundance of silver as the abundance of labour and subsistence at the disposal of those Romans, beyond what they needed for their own use. The quantity of silver they had at their disposal was a good deal less than what command over the same quantity of labour and subsistence would procure today.

Second Sort. The second kind of raw produce whose price rises as improvement advances is that which human industry can multiply in proportion to demand. It consists of those useful plants and animals which, in uncultivated countries, nature produces in such lavish abundance that they are of little or no value, and which, as cultivation advances, are therefore forced to give way to some more profitable produce. Over a long stretch of improvement, the quantity of these is continually shrinking, while at the same time the demand for them is continually growing. Their real value—the actual quantity of labour they will buy or command—therefore rises gradually, until at last it gets so high as to make them as profitable a produce as anything else human industry can raise on the most fertile and best cultivated land. Once it has got that high, it cannot well go higher. If it did, more land and more industry would soon be put to work to increase their quantity.

When the price of cattle, for example, rises so high that it is as profitable to cultivate land for their food as for man's, it cannot well go higher. If it did, more corn land would soon be turned into pasture. The spread of tillage, by reducing the amount of wild pasture, reduces the quantity of butcher's meat that the country naturally produces without labour or cultivation; and, by increasing the number of those who have corn—or, what comes to the same thing, the price of corn—to give in exchange for it, it increases the demand. The price of butcher's meat, and so of cattle, must therefore rise gradually until it gets so high that it becomes as profitable to use the most fertile and best cultivated land for raising their food as for raising corn. But it must always be late in the progress of improvement before tillage can spread far enough to raise the price of cattle to this height; and until it has reached this height, if the country is advancing at all, their price must be continually rising. There are perhaps some parts of Europe where the price of cattle has not yet reached this height. It had not reached it in any part of Scotland before the Union. Had Scottish cattle always been confined to the market of Scotland—a country where the amount of land fit for nothing but the feeding of cattle is so great in proportion to what can be used for other purposes—it is scarcely possible, perhaps, that their price could ever have risen high enough to make it profitable to cultivate land for the sake of feeding them. In England, as already noted, the price of cattle seems, around London, to have reached this height about the beginning of the last century; but it was much later, probably, before it did so through most of the remoter counties, in some of which, perhaps, it may scarcely have reached it even yet. Of all the substances making up this second kind of raw produce, however, cattle is perhaps the one whose price rises first to this height as improvement advances.

Indeed, until the price of cattle has reached this height, it seems scarcely possible that even most of the land capable of the highest cultivation can be fully cultivated. On all farms too far from a town to bring manure from it—that is, on by far the greater part of those in any large country—the amount of well-cultivated land must be in proportion to the amount of manure the farm itself produces, and this in turn must be in proportion to the stock of cattle kept on it. The land is manured either by pasturing the cattle on it or by feeding them in the stable and carting their dung out to it. But unless the price of cattle is enough to pay both the rent and the profit of cultivated land, the farmer cannot afford to pasture them on it, and still less can he afford to feed them in the stable. Cattle can be fed in the stable only with the produce of improved and cultivated land, because gathering the scanty, scattered produce of waste and unimproved land would take too much labour and be too costly. So if the price of cattle is not enough to pay for the produce of improved and cultivated land when they are allowed to pasture on it, that price will be even less able to pay for that produce when it has to be gathered with a good deal of extra labour and carried into the stable to them. In these circumstances, then, no more cattle can be fed in the stable at a profit than are needed for tillage. But these can never supply enough manure to keep constantly in good condition all the land they are capable of cultivating. What they do supply, being not enough for the whole farm, will naturally be saved for the land where it can be applied most profitably or conveniently—the most fertile, or perhaps that nearest the farmyard. This land will therefore be kept constantly in good condition and fit for tillage. The rest will, for the most part, be left to lie waste, producing scarcely anything but some wretched pasture, just enough to keep alive a few straggling, half-starved cattle; the farm, though much overstocked compared with what its full cultivation would require, is very often overstocked compared with its actual produce. A portion of this waste land, however, after being pastured in this miserable way for six or seven years together, may be ploughed up, when it will perhaps yield a poor crop or two of bad oats or some other coarse grain; then, being completely exhausted, it must be rested and pastured again as before, while another portion is ploughed up, to be in the same way exhausted and rested again in its turn. Such, indeed, was the general system of management all over the low country of Scotland before the Union. The land kept constantly well manured and in good condition seldom exceeded a third or a fourth of the whole farm, and sometimes did not amount to a fifth or a sixth of it. The rest was never manured, yet a certain portion of it was, all the same, regularly cultivated and exhausted in turn. Under this system, plainly, even that part of Scotland's land capable of good cultivation could produce but little compared with what it might be capable of producing. But however disadvantageous this system may appear, before the Union the low price of cattle seems to have made it almost unavoidable. If, despite a great rise in the price, it still prevails through a considerable part of the country, this is in many places no doubt due to ignorance and attachment to old customs, but in most places to the unavoidable obstacles which the natural course of things sets against the quick establishment of a better system: first, the poverty of the tenants, who have not yet had time to acquire a stock of cattle large enough to cultivate their land more fully—the same rise in price that would make it worth their while to keep a larger stock making it harder for them to acquire it; and secondly, their not having yet had time to put their land in condition to maintain this larger stock properly, even supposing they could acquire it. The increase of stock and the improvement of land are two things that must go hand in hand, neither of which can much outrun the other. Without some increase of stock there can be scarcely any improvement of land, but there can be no considerable increase of stock except as a result of a considerable improvement of land, since otherwise the land could not maintain it. These natural obstacles to the establishment of a better system can be removed only by a long course of thrift and industry; and half a century, or perhaps a century more, must pass before the old system, which is gradually wearing out, can be wholly abolished throughout all the different parts of the country. Of all the commercial advantages Scotland has gained from the Union with England, this rise in the price of cattle is perhaps the greatest. It has not only raised the value of all Highland estates but has perhaps been the main cause of the improvement of the low country.

In all new colonies, the great quantity of waste land that for many years can be used for nothing but the feeding of cattle soon makes them extremely abundant; and in everything great cheapness is the necessary result of great abundance. Though all the cattle of the European colonies in America were originally brought from Europe, they soon multiplied so much there, and became of so little value, that even horses were allowed to run wild in the woods without any owner thinking it worth his while to claim them. It must be a long time after the first founding of such colonies before it becomes profitable to feed cattle on the produce of cultivated land. The same causes, then—the want of manure and the mismatch between the stock used in cultivation and the land it is meant to cultivate—are likely to introduce there a system of husbandry not unlike that which still goes on in so many parts of Scotland. Mr Kalm, the Swedish traveller, in his account of the husbandry of some of the English colonies in North America as he found it in 1749, accordingly remarks that he can hardly discover there the character of the English nation, so well skilled in all the different branches of agriculture. They make scarcely any manure for their cornfields, he says; instead, when one piece of ground has been exhausted by continual cropping, they clear and cultivate another piece of fresh land, and when that is exhausted they go on to a third. Their cattle are allowed to wander through the woods and other uncultivated ground, where they are half-starved, having long ago wiped out almost all the annual grasses by cropping them too early in the spring, before they had time to flower or shed their seeds (Kalm's Travels, vol. 1, pp. 343, 344). The annual grasses, it seems, were the best natural grasses in that part of North America, and when the Europeans first settled there they used to grow very thick and rise three or four feet high. A piece of ground that, when he wrote, could not maintain one cow would in former times, he was assured, have maintained four, each of which would have given four times the milk that one was capable of giving. The poorness of the pasture had, in his opinion, caused the degradation of their cattle, which degenerated noticeably from one generation to the next. They were probably not unlike that stunted breed common all over Scotland thirty or forty years ago, which is now so much improved through most of the low country—not so much by changing the breed, though that has been done in some places, as by a more plentiful method of feeding them.

Though it is late, then, in the progress of improvement before cattle can fetch such a price as to make it profitable to cultivate land for the sake of feeding them, yet of all the different parts that make up this second kind of raw produce they are perhaps the first to fetch this price; because until they do, it seems impossible for improvement to be brought even near to the degree of perfection it has reached in many parts of Europe.

As cattle are among the first, so venison is perhaps among the last parts of this kind of raw produce to fetch this price. The price of venison in Great Britain, however extravagant it may appear, is nowhere near enough to repay the cost of a deer park, as everyone with any experience in the feeding of deer well knows. Were it otherwise, the feeding of deer would soon become an ordinary branch of farming, just as the feeding of those small birds called turdi was among the ancient Romans. Varro and Columella assure us it was a most profitable line. The fattening of ortolans, birds of passage that arrive lean in the country, is said to be so in some parts of France. If venison stays in fashion, and the wealth and luxury of Great Britain go on increasing as they have done for some time, its price may very probably rise still higher than it is at present.

Between the point in the progress of improvement that brings to its height the price of so necessary an article as cattle, and the point that does so for such a superfluity as venison, there is a very long interval, in the course of which many other kinds of raw produce gradually reach their highest price, some sooner and some later, according to different circumstances.

Thus on every farm the offals of the barn and stable will keep a certain number of poultry. Since these are fed on what would otherwise be lost, they are a pure save-all; and as they cost the farmer scarcely anything, he can afford to sell them very cheaply. Almost all he gets for them is pure gain, and their price can scarcely fall so low as to discourage him from keeping this number. But in countries that are poorly cultivated, and therefore thinly inhabited, the poultry thus raised without expense are often quite enough to supply the whole demand. In this state of things, then, they are often as cheap as butcher's meat or any other kind of animal food. But the whole quantity of poultry the farm produces in this way without expense must always be much smaller than the whole quantity of butcher's meat reared on it; and in times of wealth and luxury, what is rare, being of nearly equal merit, is always preferred to what is common. As wealth and luxury increase, then, through improvement and cultivation, the price of poultry gradually rises above that of butcher's meat, until at last it gets so high that it becomes profitable to cultivate land for the sake of feeding them. Once it has reached this height, it cannot well go higher. If it did, more land would soon be turned to this purpose. In several provinces of France the feeding of poultry is regarded as a very important branch of rural economy, and profitable enough to encourage the farmer to raise a considerable quantity of Indian corn and buckwheat for the purpose. A middling farmer there will sometimes have four hundred fowls in his yard. The feeding of poultry seems scarcely yet to be generally regarded as a matter of such importance in England. They are certainly, however, dearer in England than in France, since England draws considerable supplies from France. In the progress of improvement, the time when any particular kind of animal food is dearest must naturally be the one just before it becomes general practice to cultivate land for the sake of raising it. For some time before this practice becomes general, the scarcity must necessarily raise the price. After it has become general, new methods of feeding are commonly hit upon that let the farmer raise on the same quantity of ground a much greater quantity of that particular kind of animal food. The hog, which finds its food among filth and greedily devours many things rejected by every other useful animal, is, like poultry, originally kept as a save-all. As long as the number of such animals that can be reared at little or no expense is fully enough to supply the demand, this kind of butcher's meat comes to market at a much lower price than any other. But when the demand rises beyond what this quantity can supply, when it becomes necessary to raise food on purpose for feeding and fattening hogs, just as for other cattle, the price necessarily rises, and becomes either higher or lower than that of other butcher's meat according as the nature of the country and the state of its agriculture happen to make the feeding of hogs more or less expensive than that of other cattle. In France, according to Mr Buffon, the price of pork is nearly equal to that of beef. In most parts of Great Britain it is at present somewhat higher.

The great rise in the price of both hogs and poultry has in Great Britain often been blamed on the falling number of cottagers and other small occupiers of land—something that in every part of Europe has been the immediate forerunner of improvement and better cultivation, but that may at the same time have raised the price of these articles both somewhat sooner and somewhat faster than it otherwise would have risen. Just as the poorest family can often keep a cat or a dog at no expense, so the poorest occupiers of land can commonly keep a few poultry, or a sow and a few pigs, at very little. The little scraps from their own table—their whey, skimmed milk, and buttermilk—supply these animals with part of their food, and they find the rest in the neighbouring fields, without doing any noticeable damage to anybody. By cutting the number of these small occupiers, then, the quantity of this kind of provision, produced at little or no expense, must certainly have been a good deal reduced, and its price must consequently have been raised both sooner and faster than it otherwise would have been. Sooner or later, however, in the progress of improvement, it must at any rate have risen to the utmost height it is capable of reaching—that is, to the price that pays the labour and expense of cultivating the land which supplies them with food, as fully as these are paid on most other cultivated land.

The business of the dairy, like the feeding of hogs and poultry, is originally carried on as a save-all. The cattle necessarily kept on the farm produce more milk than either the rearing of their own young or the farmer's family requires, and they produce most at one particular season. But of all the products of the land, milk is perhaps the most perishable. In the warm season, when it is most plentiful, it will scarcely keep twenty-four hours. By making it into fresh butter the farmer stores a small part of it for a week; by making it into salt butter, for a year; and by making it into cheese, he stores a much greater part of it for several years. Part of all these is kept for his own family; the rest goes to market to find the best price to be had, which can scarcely fall so low as to discourage him from sending there whatever is over and above his family's use. If it is very low indeed, he is likely to run his dairy in a very slovenly and dirty way, and will scarcely think it worth while to have a particular room or building for it, but will let the business be carried on amid the smoke, filth, and nastiness of his own kitchen, as was the case with almost all the farmers' dairies in Scotland thirty or forty years ago, and as is still the case with many of them. The same causes that gradually raise the price of butcher's meat—the increase of demand and, as the country improves, the reduction in the quantity that can be fed at little or no expense—raise in the same way the price of the dairy's produce, whose price naturally goes with that of butcher's meat, or with the expense of feeding cattle. The higher price pays for more labour, care, and cleanliness. The dairy becomes more worthy of the farmer's attention, and the quality of its produce gradually improves. At last the price gets so high that it becomes worth while to use some of the most fertile and best cultivated land in feeding cattle solely for the dairy; and once it has reached this height, it cannot well go higher. If it did, more land would soon be turned to this purpose. It seems to have reached this height through most of England, where much good land is commonly used in this way. Except near a few considerable towns, it seems not yet to have reached this height anywhere in Scotland, where common farmers seldom use much good land in raising food for cattle solely for the dairy. The price of the produce, though it has risen very considerably within these few years, is probably still too low to allow it. The inferiority of the quality, indeed, compared with that of the produce of English dairies, fully matches that of the price. But this inferiority of quality is perhaps rather the effect of this lowness of price than the cause of it. Even if the quality were much better, most of what is brought to market could not, I suspect, in the present state of the country, be sold off at a much better price; and the present price would probably not pay the expense of the land and labour needed to produce a much better quality. Through most of England, despite the higher price, the dairy is not reckoned a more profitable use of land than the raising of corn or the fattening of cattle, the two great objects of agriculture. Through most of Scotland, then, it cannot yet be even so profitable.

The land of no country, plainly, can ever be fully cultivated and improved until once the price of every product that human industry is obliged to raise on it has got high enough to pay for the expense of complete improvement and cultivation. To do this, the price of each particular product must be enough, first, to pay the rent of good corn land, since it is that which regulates the rent of most other cultivated land; and secondly, to pay the labour and expense of the farmer as fully as they are commonly paid on good corn land—in other words, to replace, with the ordinary profits, the stock he employs about it. This rise in the price of each particular product must plainly come before the improvement and cultivation of the land meant to raise it. Gain is the end of all improvement, and nothing could deserve that name whose necessary consequence was loss. But loss must be the necessary consequence of improving land for the sake of a product whose price could never repay the expense. If the complete improvement and cultivation of the country is, as it most certainly is, the greatest of all public advantages, then this rise in the price of all those different kinds of raw produce, far from being treated as a public calamity, ought to be regarded as the necessary forerunner and companion of the greatest of all public advantages.

This rise, too, in the nominal or money price of all those different kinds of raw produce has resulted not from any debasement in the value of silver but from a rise in their real price. They have come to be worth not only a greater quantity of silver but a greater quantity of labour and subsistence than before. Just as it costs a greater quantity of labour and subsistence to bring them to market, so, once they are brought there, they represent, or are equivalent to, a greater quantity.

Third Sort. The third and last kind of raw produce whose price naturally rises as improvement advances is that in which the power of human industry to increase the quantity is either limited or uncertain. So although the real price of this kind of raw produce naturally tends to rise as improvement advances, yet according as different accidents happen to make the efforts of human industry more or less successful in increasing the quantity, it may sometimes even fall, sometimes stay the same in very different periods of improvement, and sometimes rise more or less within the same period.

There are some kinds of raw produce that nature has made a kind of appendage to other kinds, so that the quantity of the one any country can supply is necessarily limited by that of the other. The quantity of wool or of raw hides, for example, that any country can supply is necessarily limited by the number of great and small cattle kept in it. The state of its improvement, and the nature of its agriculture, in turn necessarily determine this number.

The same causes that, as improvement advances, gradually raise the price of butcher's meat might be thought to have the same effect on the prices of wool and raw hides, raising them too in nearly the same proportion. This probably would be so if, in the rude beginnings of improvement, the market for the latter goods were as narrowly bounded as that for the former. But the extent of their respective markets is commonly very different.

The market for butcher's meat is almost everywhere confined to the country that produces it. Ireland and some part of British America, it is true, carry on a considerable trade in salt provisions; but they are, I believe, the only countries in the commercial world that do so, or that export to other countries any considerable part of their butcher's meat.

The market for wool and raw hides, on the contrary, is in the rude beginnings of improvement very seldom confined to the country that produces them. They can easily be carried to distant countries—wool without any preparation, and raw hides with very little; and since they are the materials of many manufactures, the industry of other countries may create a demand for them even where that of the country producing them might create none.

In countries that are poorly cultivated, and therefore thinly inhabited, the price of the wool and the hide always bears a much greater proportion to that of the whole beast than in countries where, improvement and population being further advanced, there is more demand for butcher's meat. Mr Hume observes that in Saxon times the fleece was reckoned at two-fifths of the value of the whole sheep, and that this was much above the proportion of its present valuation. In some provinces of Spain, I have been assured, the sheep is often killed merely for the sake of the fleece and the tallow. The carcase is often left to rot on the ground or to be devoured by beasts and birds of prey. If this sometimes happens even in Spain, it happens almost constantly in Chile, at Buenos Ayres, and in many other parts of Spanish America, where the horned cattle are almost constantly killed merely for the sake of the hide and the tallow. This too used to happen almost constantly in Hispaniola, while it was infested by the buccaneers, and before the settlement, improvement, and populousness of the French plantations—which now extend round the coast of almost the whole western half of the island—had given some value to the cattle of the Spaniards, who still continue to hold not only the eastern part of the coast but the whole inland mountainous part of the country.

Though, as improvement and population advance, the price of the whole beast necessarily rises, yet the price of the carcase is likely to be far more affected by this rise than that of the wool and the hide. The market for the carcase, being in the rude state of society always confined to the country that produces it, must necessarily expand in proportion to the improvement and population of that country. But the market for the wool and the hides, even of a barbarous country, often extending to the whole commercial world, can very seldom be enlarged in the same proportion. The state of the whole commercial world can seldom be much affected by the improvement of any particular country, and the market for such goods may remain the same, or very nearly the same, after such improvements as before. It ought, however, in the natural course of things, on the whole to be somewhat enlarged as a result of them. If the manufactures, especially, of which these goods are the materials, should ever come to flourish in the country, the market, though it might not be much enlarged, would at least be brought much nearer the place of growth than before; and the price of those materials might at least be raised by what had usually been the cost of carrying them to distant countries. So although it might not rise in the same proportion as that of butcher's meat, it ought naturally to rise somewhat, and it certainly ought not to fall.

In England, however, despite the flourishing state of its woollen manufacture, the price of English wool has fallen very considerably since the time of Edward III. Many authentic records show that during the reign of that prince—towards the middle of the fourteenth century, or about 1339—what was reckoned the moderate and reasonable price of the tod, or twenty-eight pounds, of English wool was not less than ten shillings of the money of those times (see Smith's Memoirs of Wool, vol. i, c. 5, 6, 7, and vol. ii), containing, at twenty pence the ounce, six ounces of silver, Tower weight, equal to about thirty shillings of our present money. At present, twenty-one shillings the tod may be reckoned a good price for very good English wool. The money price of wool in the time of Edward III was therefore to its money price at present as ten to seven. The advantage in its real price was greater still. At six shillings and eightpence the quarter, ten shillings was in those ancient times the price of twelve bushels of wheat. At twenty-eight shillings the quarter, twenty-one shillings is at present the price of only six bushels. The proportion between the real price of ancient and modern times is therefore as twelve to six, or two to one. In those ancient times a tod of wool would have bought twice the quantity of subsistence it will buy at present, and consequently twice the quantity of labour, if the real reward of labour had been the same in both periods.

This fall, both in the real and the nominal value of wool, could never have happened in the natural course of things. It has accordingly been the effect of force and contrivance. First, of the absolute ban on exporting wool from England; secondly, of the permission to import it from Spain duty-free; thirdly, of the ban on exporting it from Ireland to any country but England. As a result of these regulations, the market for English wool, instead of being somewhat enlarged by the improvement of England, has been confined to the home market, where the wool of several other countries is allowed to compete with it, and where that of Ireland is forced to compete with it. And since the woollen manufactures of Ireland, too, are discouraged as fully as is consistent with justice and fair dealing, the Irish can work up but a smaller part of their own wool at home, and are therefore obliged to send a greater proportion of it to Great Britain, the only market they are allowed.

I have not been able to find any such authentic records for the price of raw hides in ancient times. Wool was commonly paid as a subsidy to the king, and its valuation in that subsidy fixes, at least to some degree, what its ordinary price was. But this does not seem to have been the case with raw hides. Fleetwood, however, from an account in 1425 between the prior of Burcester Oxford and one of his canons, gives us their price, at least as stated on that particular occasion, namely: five ox hides at twelve shillings; five cow hides at seven shillings and threepence; thirty-six sheep skins of two years old at nine shillings; sixteen calf skins at two shillings. In 1425, twelve shillings contained about the same quantity of silver as twenty-four shillings of our present money. An ox hide, therefore, was in this account valued at the same quantity of silver as 4s. ⅔ of our present money. Its nominal price was a good deal lower than at present. But at six shillings and eightpence the quarter, twelve shillings would in those times have bought fourteen bushels and four-fifths of a bushel of wheat, which at three and sixpence the bushel would at present cost 51s. 4d. An ox hide, therefore, would in those times have bought as much corn as ten shillings and threepence would buy at present. Its real value was equal to ten shillings and threepence of our present money. In those ancient times, when the cattle were half-starved through most of the winter, we cannot suppose they were of a very large size. An ox hide weighing four stone of sixteen pounds avoirdupois is not at present reckoned a bad one, and in those ancient times would probably have been reckoned a very good one. But at half-a-crown the stone, which at this moment (February 1773) I understand to be the common price, such a hide would at present cost only ten shillings. So although its nominal price is higher now than in those ancient times, its real price—the actual quantity of subsistence it will buy or command—is rather somewhat lower. The price of cow hides, as stated in the above account, is nearly in the usual proportion to that of ox hides. That of sheep skins is a good deal above it. They had probably been sold with the wool. That of calf skins, on the contrary, is greatly below it. In countries where the price of cattle is very low, the calves not meant to be reared to keep up the stock are generally killed very young, as was the case in Scotland twenty or thirty years ago. It saves the milk, which their price would not pay for. Their skins, therefore, are commonly good for little.

The price of raw hides is a good deal lower at present than it was a few years ago, owing probably to the removal of the duty on seal skins and to the allowing, for a limited time, of the import of raw hides from Ireland and from the plantations duty-free, which was done in 1769. Take the whole of the present century on average, and their real price has probably been somewhat higher than it was in those ancient times. The nature of the commodity makes it not quite so fit for being carried to distant markets as wool. It suffers more by keeping. A salted hide is reckoned inferior to a fresh one and sells for a lower price. This circumstance must necessarily tend somewhat to lower the price of raw hides produced in a country that does not manufacture them but is obliged to export them, and comparatively to raise that of those produced in a country that does manufacture them. It must tend to lower their price in a barbarous country and to raise it in an improved and manufacturing one. It must therefore have tended to lower it in ancient times and to raise it in modern ones. Our tanners, besides, have not been quite so successful as our clothiers in convincing the wisdom of the nation that the safety of the commonwealth depends on the prosperity of their particular manufacture. They have accordingly been much less favoured. The export of raw hides has indeed been banned and declared a nuisance, but their import from foreign countries has been subjected to a duty; and though this duty has been taken off those of Ireland and the plantations (for the limited time of five years only), yet Ireland has not been confined to the market of Great Britain for the sale of its surplus hides, or of those not manufactured at home. The hides of common cattle have only within these few years been put among the enumerated commodities which the plantations can send nowhere but to the mother country; nor has the commerce of Ireland in this case been oppressed hitherto in order to support the manufactures of Great Britain.

Whatever regulations tend to push the price of either wool or raw hides below what it naturally would be must, in an improved and cultivated country, tend somewhat to raise the price of butcher's meat. The price of both the great and small cattle fed on improved and cultivated land must be enough to pay the rent the landlord, and the profit the farmer, has reason to expect from improved and cultivated land. If it is not, they will soon stop feeding them. Whatever part of this price, then, is not paid by the wool and the hide must be paid by the carcase. The less is paid for the one, the more must be paid for the other. In what way this price is divided among the different parts of the beast is a matter of indifference to landlords and farmers, provided it is all paid to them. In an improved and cultivated country, then, their interest as landlords and farmers cannot be much affected by such regulations, though their interest as consumers may be, through the rise in the price of provisions. It would be quite otherwise, however, in an unimproved and uncultivated country, where most of the land could be used for nothing but the feeding of cattle, and where the wool and the hide made up the chief part of the value of those cattle. There their interest as landlords and farmers would be very deeply affected by such regulations, and their interest as consumers very little. The fall in the price of the wool and the hide would not in this case raise the price of the carcase; because, most of the country's land being fit for nothing but the feeding of cattle, the same number would still be fed. The same quantity of butcher's meat would still come to market. The demand for it would be no greater than before. Its price, therefore, would be the same as before. The whole price of cattle would fall, and along with it both the rent and the profit of all those lands of which cattle was the chief produce—that is, of most of the country's land. The perpetual ban on the export of wool, which is commonly but very falsely ascribed to Edward III, would, in the circumstances of the country at that time, have been the most destructive regulation that could well have been devised. It would not only have reduced the actual value of most of the land in the kingdom but, by lowering the price of the most important kind of small cattle, would have greatly retarded its later improvement.

After Scotland's union with England, the price of Scottish wool dropped sharply. The union shut Scottish wool out of the large European market and confined it to the smaller market of Great Britain. Most of the land in the southern counties of Scotland is sheep country, so this would have hit its value very hard. What saved it was the rise in the price of butcher's meat, which fully made up for the fall in the price of wool.

Human industry has only a limited power to increase the supply of wool or raw hides, because that power depends on what the home country itself produces. And it is uncertain as well, because it also depends on the produce of other countries. What matters there is not so much how much those countries produce as how much they leave unmanufactured, together with whatever restraints they may or may not choose to place on exporting this kind of raw produce. Since these conditions have nothing to do with domestic industry, they inevitably make its results more or less uncertain. So when it comes to multiplying this sort of raw produce, the power of human industry is not only limited but uncertain.

In multiplying another very important kind of raw produce, the quantity of fish brought to market, the power of human industry is likewise both limited and uncertain. It is limited by where the country sits: by how near or far its various provinces are from the sea, by how many lakes and rivers it has, and by what you might call the richness or poverty of those seas, lakes, and rivers in this kind of produce. As the population grows, and as the country's annual produce of land and labour gets larger and larger, there come to be more buyers of fish; and those buyers also have a greater quantity and variety of other goods, or, what amounts to the same thing, the price of a greater quantity and variety of other goods, to buy with. But it is generally impossible to supply this large, extended market without employing more labour, in proportion, than was needed to supply the small, confined one. A market that once needed only one thousand tons of fish a year and comes to need ten thousand can seldom be supplied without employing more than ten times the labour that used to be enough. The fish must usually be sought further out, larger vessels must be used, and more expensive equipment of every kind brought into play. So the real price of fish naturally rises as a country improves. I believe it has in fact done so, to a greater or lesser degree, in every country.

The success of any single day's fishing may be very uncertain. But once you fix the country's location, the general power of industry to bring a given quantity of fish to market, averaged over a year or several years together, may perhaps be thought certain enough, and no doubt it is. Yet because this power depends more on where the country sits than on the state of its wealth and industry, it can be the same in different countries at very different stages of improvement, and very different in the same country at the same stage. Its link to the state of improvement is therefore uncertain, and it is this kind of uncertainty that I am talking about here.

When it comes to increasing the supply of the various minerals and metals dug out of the earth, and the more precious ones in particular, the power of human industry seems not so much limited as wholly uncertain.

How much of the precious metals a country has is not limited by anything in its location, such as the richness or poverty of its own mines. These metals are often plentiful in countries that have no mines at all. The amount in any particular country seems to depend on two different things. First, on its buying power: on the state of its industry and on the annual produce of its land and labour, which determines how much labour and subsistence it can afford to spend in obtaining or buying luxuries like gold and silver, whether from its own mines or from those of other countries. Second, on the richness or poverty of whichever mines happen at any given time to supply the commercial world with these metals. Even in the countries furthest from the mines, the amount must be affected to some degree by that richness or poverty, because these metals are easy and cheap to transport, being small in bulk and great in value. The amount in China and Hindustan must have been affected to some degree by the abundance of the mines of America.

Insofar as the amount in any particular country depends on the first of these two things, its buying power, the real price of these metals, like that of all other luxuries, is likely to rise as the country grows wealthier and more improved, and to fall as it grows poorer and more depressed. Countries with a large surplus of labour and subsistence can afford to buy a given quantity of these metals at the cost of more labour and subsistence than countries with less to spare.

Insofar as the amount in any particular country depends on the second of these two things, the richness or poverty of the mines that happen to supply the commercial world, the real price of these metals, meaning the real quantity of labour and subsistence they will buy or exchange for, will of course fall more or less in proportion to how rich those mines are, and rise in proportion to how poor they are.

But the richness or poverty of the mines that happen at any given time to supply the commercial world clearly may have no connection at all with the state of industry in any particular country. It does not even seem to have any necessary connection with the state of the world in general. As the arts and commerce gradually spread over a larger and larger part of the earth, the search for new mines covers a wider surface and so may have a somewhat better chance of success than when it was confined to narrower bounds. Even so, discovering new mines as the old ones gradually run out is a matter of the greatest uncertainty, and one that no human skill or industry can guarantee. Every sign of a mine, it is admitted, is doubtful; only actually finding a new mine and working it successfully can establish that its value, or even its existence, is real. In this search there seem to be no fixed limits to how far human industry may succeed, or how far it may be disappointed. Within a century or two, new mines may be discovered that are richer than any yet known; and it is just as possible that the richest mine then known may be poorer than any worked before America's mines were found. Which of these two outcomes happens matters very little to the real wealth and prosperity of the world, or to the real value of the annual produce of mankind's land and labour. Its nominal value, the quantity of gold and silver it could be expressed in, would of course be very different; but its real value, the real quantity of labour it could buy or command, would be exactly the same. In the one case a shilling might stand for no more labour than a penny does now; in the other, a penny might stand for as much as a shilling does now. But in the first case the man with a shilling in his pocket would be no richer than the man with a penny is today; and in the second, the man with a penny would be just as rich as the man with a shilling now. Cheap and plentiful gold and silver plate would be the only benefit the world could get from the first outcome, and dear and scarce gold and silver plate, those trifling luxuries, the only inconvenience it could suffer from the second.
Conclusion of the Digression Concerning the Variations in the Value of Silver

Most of the writers who have gathered the money prices of things in ancient times seem to have treated the low money price of corn, and of goods in general, or in other words the high value of gold and silver, as proof not only that these metals were scarce but that the country was poor and barbarous at the time. This notion belongs to the system of political economy that equates national wealth with an abundance of gold and silver and national poverty with a scarcity of them, a system I shall try to explain and examine at length in the fourth book of this Inquiry. For now I will only point out that a high value of the precious metals can be no proof that any particular country was poor or barbarous at the time. It proves only that the mines which happened to supply the commercial world at that time were poor. A poor country, just as it cannot afford to buy more gold and silver, can as little afford to pay more for it than a rich country can; so the value of these metals is not likely to be higher in the poor country than in the rich one. In China, a country much richer than any part of Europe, the value of the precious metals is much higher than anywhere in Europe. As Europe's wealth has grown greatly since the discovery of America's mines, the value of gold and silver there has gradually fallen. But this fall in their value has not been due to any increase in Europe's real wealth, in the annual produce of its land and labour; it has been due to the accidental discovery of richer mines than any known before. The increase in the quantity of gold and silver in Europe and the growth of its manufactures and agriculture are two events that, though they happened at roughly the same time, arose from very different causes and have scarcely any natural connection with each other. The first arose from a mere accident, in which neither prudence nor policy had, or could have had, any part; the second arose from the fall of the feudal system and the establishment of a government that gave industry the one encouragement it needs, some tolerable security that it will enjoy the fruits of its own labour. Poland, where the feudal system still survives, is to this day as poor a country as it was before the discovery of America. Yet the money price of corn has risen there too; the real value of the precious metals has fallen in Poland, just as in the rest of Europe. So their quantity must have increased there as elsewhere, and in roughly the same proportion to the annual produce of its land and labour. Yet this increase in the quantity of the metals has clearly not increased that annual produce, has not improved the country's manufactures or agriculture, and has not bettered the condition of its people. Spain and Portugal, the countries that own the mines, are, after Poland, perhaps the two poorest countries in Europe. Yet the value of the precious metals must be lower in Spain and Portugal than anywhere else in Europe, since they leave those countries for all other parts of Europe loaded not only with freight and insurance but with the cost of smuggling, their export being either banned or taxed. In proportion to the annual produce of land and labour, then, their quantity must be greater in those countries than anywhere else in Europe; yet those countries are poorer than most of Europe. The feudal system has been abolished in Spain and Portugal, but what replaced it is not much better.

So just as a low value of gold and silver is no proof that the country where it occurs is wealthy and flourishing, neither is a high value of these metals, or a low money price of goods in general, or of corn in particular, any proof that the country is poor and barbarous.

But although a low money price of goods in general, or of corn in particular, is no proof that the times were poor or barbarous, a low money price of certain particular goods, such as cattle, poultry, and game of all kinds, relative to the price of corn, is a most decisive proof of it. It clearly shows, first, that these goods were very abundant relative to corn, and therefore that the land they occupied was very large relative to the land under corn; and second, that this land was of low value relative to corn land, and therefore that by far the greater part of the country's land was uncultivated and unimproved. It clearly shows that the country's stock and population did not bear the same proportion to the extent of its territory as they commonly do in civilized countries, and that society in that country was at that time still in its infancy. From the high or low money price of goods in general, or of corn in particular, we can infer only that the mines which happened at the time to supply the commercial world with gold and silver were rich or poor, not that the country was rich or poor. But from the high or low money price of some kinds of goods relative to others, we can infer, with a probability that comes almost to certainty, whether the country was rich or poor, whether most of its land was improved or unimproved, and whether it was in a more or less barbarous state, or a more or less civilized one.

Any rise in the money price of goods that came entirely from a fall in the value of silver would affect all kinds of goods equally and raise their prices across the board, by a third, or a fourth, or a fifth, according as silver happened to lose a third, a fourth, or a fifth of its former value. But the rise in the price of provisions, which has been the subject of so much reasoning and conversation, does not affect all kinds of provisions equally. Even those who explain this rise by a fall in the value of silver admit that, taken on average over the present century, the price of corn has risen much less than the price of some other provisions. So the rise in the price of those other provisions cannot be due entirely to a fall in the value of silver. Some other causes must be taken into account; and the ones set out above will perhaps explain this rise in those particular provisions whose price has actually risen relative to corn, without our having to fall back on the supposed fall in the value of silver.

As for the price of corn itself, during the first sixty-four years of the present century, and before the recent extraordinary run of bad seasons, it was somewhat lower than during the last sixty-four years of the previous century. This is confirmed not only by the records of Windsor market, but by the public fiars of all the different counties of Scotland, and by the records of several different markets in France, which Mr Messance and Mr Dupré de St Maur have collected with great diligence and care. The evidence is more complete than one could well have expected in a matter so naturally hard to establish.
As for the high price of corn over these last ten or twelve years, it can be fully explained by the bad seasons, without supposing any fall in the value of silver.
The opinion, then, that silver is steadily falling in value does not seem to rest on any sound observation, whether of the prices of corn or of other provisions.

It may perhaps be said that, even on the account I have given here, the same quantity of silver will today buy a much smaller quantity of several kinds of provisions than it would have done during part of the last century; and that to ask whether this change is due to a rise in the value of those goods or to a fall in the value of silver is merely to set up a pointless distinction, of no use whatever to the man who has only a fixed quantity of silver to take to market, or a fixed money income. I certainly do not claim that grasping this distinction will let him buy any cheaper. But it may not be entirely useless on that account.

It may be of some use to the public by giving an easy proof of the country's prosperity. If the rise in the price of some kinds of provisions is due entirely to a fall in the value of silver, it is due to something from which nothing can be inferred except that the American mines are rich. Despite this, the country's real wealth, the annual produce of its land and labour, may be either gradually declining, as in Portugal and Poland, or gradually advancing, as in most other parts of Europe. But if this rise in the price of some kinds of provisions is due to a rise in the real value of the land that produces them, to its increased fertility, or to its having been made fit to grow corn through more extensive improvement and good cultivation, then it is due to something that shows, in the clearest way, that the country is prosperous and advancing. Land makes up by far the greatest, most important, and most lasting part of the wealth of every large country. So it may surely be of some use, or at least give the public some satisfaction, to have such decisive proof that the value of by far the greatest, most important, and most lasting part of its wealth is rising.

It may also be of some use to the public in setting the pay of some of its lower servants. If this rise in the price of some kinds of provisions is due to a fall in the value of silver, then their pay, provided it was not too large already, ought certainly to be raised in proportion to the fall. If it is not raised, their real reward will plainly be cut by that much. But if the rise in price is due to the increased value of the land that produces such provisions, from its improved fertility, then it becomes a much finer matter to judge in what proportion any pay ought to be raised, or whether it ought to be raised at all. As improvement and cultivation spread, they necessarily raise the price of every kind of animal food more or less in line with the price of corn, while just as necessarily lowering the price of, I believe, every kind of vegetable food. They raise the price of animal food because much of the land that produces it, having been made fit to grow corn, must yield the landlord and farmer the rent and profit of corn land. They lower the price of vegetable food because, by making the land more fertile, they make it more abundant. Improvements in agriculture also bring in many kinds of vegetable food that, needing less land and no more labour than corn, come to market much more cheaply. Such are potatoes and maize, or what is called Indian corn, the two most important improvements that the agriculture of Europe, perhaps that Europe itself, has gained from the great extension of its commerce and navigation. Besides this, many kinds of vegetable food that in the crude state of agriculture are confined to the kitchen garden and raised only with the spade come, in its improved state, to be grown in common fields and raised with the plough, such as turnips, carrots, and cabbages. So as a country improves, if the real price of one kind of food necessarily rises, that of another necessarily falls; and it becomes a finer matter to judge how far the rise in the one is made up for by the fall in the other. Once the real price of butcher's meat has reached its peak, which for every kind except perhaps pork it seems to have done across much of England more than a century ago, any later rise in the price of any other kind of animal food cannot much affect the condition of the lower ranks of people. The condition of the poor across much of England surely cannot be as distressed by any rise in the price of poultry, fish, wildfowl, or venison as it must be relieved by the fall in the price of potatoes.

In the present season of scarcity, the high price of corn no doubt distresses the poor. But in times of moderate plenty, when corn is at its ordinary or average price, the natural rise in the price of any other kind of raw produce cannot much affect them. They suffer more, perhaps, from the artificial rise that taxes have caused in the price of certain manufactured goods, such as salt, soap, leather, candles, malt, beer, and ale.
Effects of the Progress of Improvement upon the Real Price of Manufactures

The natural effect of improvement, however, is to lower gradually the real price of almost all manufactures. The real price of the manufacturing workmanship falls, perhaps, in every one of them without exception. Thanks to better machinery, greater skill, and a better division and arrangement of the work, all of which are the natural effects of improvement, much less labour comes to be needed to carry out any particular piece of work; and although the real price of labour may rise considerably as society flourishes, the great reduction in the quantity of labour needed will generally far more than make up for the greatest rise that can happen in its price.

There are, it is true, a few manufactures in which the necessary rise in the real price of the raw materials will more than make up for all the advantages improvement can bring to the work itself. In the work of carpenters and joiners, and in the coarser sort of cabinet-making, the necessary rise in the real price of timber, which follows from the improvement of land, will more than make up for all the advantages that can come from the best machinery, the greatest skill, and the best division and arrangement of the work.
But in every case where the real price of the raw material either does not rise at all, or does not rise much, the price of the manufactured good falls considerably.

This fall in price has, over the present and the previous century, been most striking in those manufactures whose materials are the coarser metals. A better watch movement than could have been bought for twenty pounds around the middle of the last century may now perhaps be had for twenty shillings. In the work of cutlers and locksmiths, in all the toys made of the coarser metals, and in all the goods commonly known as Birmingham and Sheffield ware, there has been over the same period a very great reduction in price, though not quite so great as in watchmaking. It has, however, been enough to astonish the workmen of every other part of Europe, who in many cases admit that they cannot produce work of equal quality for double or even triple the price. There are perhaps no manufactures in which the division of labour can be carried further, or in which the machinery used admits of a greater variety of improvements, than those whose materials are the coarser metals.

In the clothing manufacture there has been no such noticeable reduction in price over the same period. On the contrary, I have been assured that the price of superfine cloth has, within the last twenty-five or thirty years, risen somewhat in proportion to its quality, owing, it was said, to a considerable rise in the price of the material, which is entirely Spanish wool. The price of Yorkshire cloth, which is made entirely of English wool, is said to have fallen a good deal in proportion to its quality over the present century. But quality is so disputable a matter that I regard all information of this kind as somewhat uncertain. In the clothing manufacture, the division of labour is nearly the same now as it was a century ago, and the machinery used is not very different. There may, however, have been some small improvements in both, which may have brought about some reduction in price.

But the reduction becomes much more noticeable and undeniable if we compare the price of this manufacture today with what it was at a much more distant period, towards the end of the fifteenth century, when the labour was probably much less subdivided and the machinery used much more primitive than it is now.

In 1487, the fourth year of Henry VII, a law was passed that “whoever shall sell by retail a broad yard of the finest scarlet grained, or of other grained cloth of the finest making, above sixteen shillings, shall forfeit forty shillings for every yard so sold.” Sixteen shillings, which contained about the same quantity of silver as twenty-four shillings of our present money, was therefore reckoned at that time not an unreasonable price for a yard of the finest cloth; and since this is a sumptuary law, such cloth had probably usually sold somewhat dearer. A guinea may be reckoned the highest price today. So even if we suppose the quality of the cloths to be equal, and the cloth of the present day is most likely much better, even on that supposition the money price of the finest cloth appears to have fallen considerably since the end of the fifteenth century. But its real price has fallen much more. Six shillings and eightpence was then, and long afterwards, reckoned the average price of a quarter of wheat. Sixteen shillings was therefore the price of more than two quarters and three bushels of wheat. Valuing a quarter of wheat today at twenty-eight shillings, the real price of a yard of fine cloth must in those times have been equal to at least three pounds six shillings and sixpence of our present money. The man who bought it must have given up command over a quantity of labour and subsistence equal to what that sum would buy today.
The reduction in the real price of the coarse manufacture, though considerable, has not been as great as in the fine.

In 1463, the third year of Edward IV, a law was passed that “no servant in husbandry, nor common labourer, nor servant to any artificer living outside a city or borough, shall use or wear in their clothing any cloth above two shillings the broad yard.” In the third year of Edward IV, two shillings contained very nearly the same quantity of silver as four shillings of our present money. But the Yorkshire cloth now sold at four shillings the yard is probably much better than any made then for the wear of the very poorest order of common servants. So even the money price of their clothing may, in proportion to its quality, be somewhat cheaper now than it was in those ancient times. The real price is certainly a good deal cheaper. Tenpence was then reckoned the so-called moderate and reasonable price of a bushel of wheat. Two shillings was therefore the price of two bushels and nearly two pecks of wheat, which today, at three shillings and sixpence the bushel, would be worth eight shillings and ninepence. For a yard of this cloth the poor servant must have given up the power to buy a quantity of subsistence equal to what eight shillings and ninepence would buy today. This too is a sumptuary law, restraining the luxury and extravagance of the poor. So their clothing had commonly been much more expensive.

The same order of people are, by the same law, forbidden to wear hose costing more than fourteen pence the pair, equal to about twenty-eight pence of our present money. But fourteen pence was in those times the price of a bushel and nearly two pecks of wheat, which today, at three shillings and sixpence the bushel, would cost five shillings and threepence. Today we should consider this a very high price for a pair of stockings for a servant of the poorest and lowest order. Yet in those times he must have paid what was really equivalent to this price for them.

In the time of Edward IV the art of knitting stockings was probably unknown anywhere in Europe. Their hose were made of ordinary cloth, which may have been one reason for their high price. The first person to wear stockings in England is said to have been Queen Elizabeth. She received them as a present from the Spanish ambassador.

In both the coarse and the fine woollen manufacture, the machinery used was much more primitive in those ancient times than it is now. Since then it has received three very major improvements, besides probably many smaller ones whose number and importance may be hard to establish. The three major improvements are these. First, the replacement of the distaff and spindle by the spinning-wheel, which with the same amount of labour will do more than twice the work. Second, the use of several very ingenious machines that make the winding of the worsted and woollen yarn, or the proper arrangement of the warp and weft before they go into the loom, far easier and quicker; before these machines were invented, this work must have been extremely tedious and troublesome. Third, the use of the fulling-mill to thicken the cloth, instead of treading it in water. No wind or water mills of any kind were known in England as early as the start of the sixteenth century, nor, so far as I know, anywhere else in Europe north of the Alps. They had been introduced into Italy some time before.

Considering these circumstances may perhaps help to explain to us why the real price of both the coarse and the fine manufacture was so much higher in those ancient times than it is now. It took more labour to bring the goods to market. So when they were brought there, they must have bought, or exchanged for the price of, a greater quantity of other things.

The coarse manufacture in those ancient times was probably carried on in England in the same way it has always been in countries where the arts and manufactures are in their infancy. It was probably a household manufacture, in which every different part of the work was done now and then by all the different members of almost every private family, but only as something they did when they had nothing else to do, not as the main business from which any of them got the greater part of their living. Work done in this way, as already noted, always comes to market much more cheaply than work that is the main or sole source of the worker's living. The fine manufacture, on the other hand, was in those times carried on not in England but in the rich, commercial country of Flanders; and it was probably conducted then, as now, by people who got the whole or the main part of their living from it. It was, besides, a foreign manufacture, and must have paid some duty, at least the ancient custom of tonnage and poundage, to the king. This duty, however, was probably not very great. It was not then the policy of Europe to restrain the import of foreign manufactures with high duties, but rather to encourage it, so that merchants could supply the great men as cheaply as possible with the comforts and luxuries they wanted, which their own country's industry could not provide.

Considering these circumstances may perhaps help to explain to us why, in those ancient times, the real price of the coarse manufacture was so much lower in proportion to that of the fine than it is today.
Conclusion of the Chapter

I shall end this very long chapter by observing that every improvement in the condition of society tends, directly or indirectly, to raise the real rent of land, to increase the real wealth of the landlord, his power to buy the labour, or the produce of the labour, of other people.
The spread of improvement and cultivation raises it directly. The landlord's share of the produce necessarily grows as the produce grows.

That rise in the real price of those parts of the raw produce of land, which is at first the effect of more extensive improvement and cultivation, and afterwards the cause of their being extended still further, the rise in the price of cattle, for example, also tends to raise the rent of land directly, and in a still greater proportion. The real value of the landlord's share, his real command over the labour of other people, not only rises with the real value of the produce, but his share itself becomes a larger proportion of the whole produce.

That produce, after the rise in its real price, takes no more labour to gather than before. So a smaller proportion of it will be enough to replace, with the usual profit, the stock that employs that labour. A greater proportion of it must therefore go to the landlord.

All those improvements in the productive powers of labour that tend directly to lower the real price of manufactures tend indirectly to raise the real rent of land. The landlord exchanges that part of his raw produce which is over and above his own consumption, or, what comes to the same thing, the price of that part, for manufactured goods. Whatever lowers the real price of the manufactured goods raises that of the raw produce. An equal quantity of the raw produce thereby becomes worth a greater quantity of the manufactured goods, and the landlord is able to buy a greater quantity of the comforts, ornaments, or luxuries he needs.

Every increase in the real wealth of society, every increase in the quantity of useful labour employed within it, tends indirectly to raise the real rent of land. A certain proportion of this labour naturally goes to the land. More men and cattle are employed in cultivating it, the produce grows with the increase of the stock thus employed in raising it, and the rent grows with the produce.

The opposite circumstances, the neglect of cultivation and improvement, the fall in the real price of any part of the raw produce of land, the rise in the real price of manufactures from the decay of manufacturing skill and industry, the decline in the real wealth of society, all tend, on the other hand, to lower the real rent of land, to reduce the real wealth of the landlord, and to diminish his power to buy either the labour, or the produce of the labour, of other people.

The whole annual produce of the land and labour of every country, or, what comes to the same thing, the whole price of that annual produce, naturally divides itself, as already noted, into three parts: the rent of land, the wages of labour, and the profits of stock; and it forms a revenue for three different orders of people: those who live by rent, those who live by wages, and those who live by profit. These are the three great, original, and constituent orders of every civilized society, from whose revenue that of every other order is ultimately derived.

The interest of the first of these three great orders, it appears from what has just been said, is strictly and inseparably bound up with the general interest of society. Whatever promotes or obstructs the one necessarily promotes or obstructs the other. When the public deliberates over any regulation of commerce or policy, the proprietors of land can never mislead it in order to promote the interest of their own particular order, at least if they have any tolerable knowledge of that interest. They are, indeed, too often lacking in even this tolerable knowledge. They are the only one of the three orders whose revenue costs them neither labour nor care, but comes to them, as it were, of its own accord, independent of any plan or project of their own. The indolence that naturally results from the ease and security of their position too often makes them not only ignorant but incapable of the mental application needed to foresee and understand the consequences of any public regulation.

The interest of the second order, those who live by wages, is as strictly bound up with the interest of society as that of the first. The labourer's wages, as already shown, are never so high as when the demand for labour is steadily rising, or when the quantity employed grows considerably every year. When this real wealth of society becomes stationary, his wages are soon cut down to what is barely enough to let him raise a family, or to keep the race of labourers going. When society declines, his wages fall even below this. The order of proprietors may perhaps gain more from the prosperity of society than the order of labourers does; but no order suffers so cruelly from its decline. And although the labourer's interest is strictly bound up with that of society, he is incapable either of grasping that interest or of understanding how it connects with his own. His condition leaves him no time to get the necessary information, and his education and habits are usually such as to make him unfit to judge even if he were fully informed. So in the public deliberations his voice is little heard and less regarded, except on certain occasions when his clamour is stirred up, egged on, and backed by his employers, not for his purposes but for their own.

His employers make up the third order, those who live by profit. It is the stock employed for the sake of profit that sets in motion the greater part of the useful labour of every society. The plans and projects of the employers of stock regulate and direct all the most important operations of labour, and profit is the end aimed at by all those plans and projects. But the rate of profit does not, like rent and wages, rise with the prosperity and fall with the decline of society. On the contrary, it is naturally low in rich countries and high in poor ones, and it is always highest in the countries going fastest to ruin. So the interest of this third order has not the same connection with the general interest of society as that of the other two. In this order, merchants and master manufacturers are the two classes of people who commonly employ the largest capitals, and who by their wealth draw to themselves the greatest share of public consideration. Since they are engaged all their lives in plans and projects, they often have sharper understanding than most country gentlemen. But because their thoughts are usually fixed on the interest of their own particular branch of business rather than on that of society, their judgment, even when given with the greatest candour (which it has not been on every occasion), is far more to be trusted on the first of these two objects than on the second. Their superiority over the country gentleman lies not so much in their knowledge of the public interest as in their better knowledge of their own interest than he has of his. It is by this superior knowledge of their own interest that they have often imposed on his generosity, and persuaded him to give up both his own interest and that of the public, out of a very simple but honest conviction that their interest, and not his, was the interest of the public. But the interest of the dealers in any particular branch of trade or manufactures is always in some respects different from, and even opposite to, that of the public. To widen the market and to narrow the competition is always the interest of the dealers. To widen the market may often be agreeable enough to the public interest; but to narrow the competition must always be against it, and can only enable the dealers, by raising their profits above what they would naturally be, to levy for their own benefit an absurd tax on the rest of their fellow citizens. Any proposal for a new law or regulation of commerce that comes from this order ought always to be listened to with great caution, and ought never to be adopted until it has been long and carefully examined, not only with the most scrupulous but with the most suspicious attention. It comes from an order of men whose interest is never exactly the same as that of the public, who generally have an interest in deceiving and even oppressing the public, and who accordingly have, on many occasions, both deceived and oppressed it.
