BOOK II. OF THE NATURE, ACCUMULATION, AND EMPLOYMENT OF STOCK.
INTRODUCTION

In that crude state of society where there is no division of labour, where exchanges are seldom made, and where every man provides everything for himself, there is no need for any stock to be accumulated or stored up in advance to carry on the business of society. Every man tries to supply his own occasional wants by his own labour, as they arise. When he is hungry, he goes to the forest to hunt; when his coat wears out, he clothes himself in the skin of the first large animal he kills; and when his hut starts falling apart, he repairs it as best he can with the trees and turf nearest to hand.

But once the division of labour has been thoroughly introduced, the produce of a man's own labour can supply only a very small part of his occasional wants. By far the greater part of them are supplied by the produce of other men's labour, which he buys with the produce, or, what is the same thing, with the price of the produce, of his own. But he cannot make this purchase until the produce of his own labour has not only been finished but sold. A stock of goods of various kinds must therefore be stored up somewhere, enough to keep him going and to supply him with the materials and tools of his work, at least until both these things can be brought about. A weaver cannot devote himself entirely to his particular business unless there is stored up in advance somewhere, either in his own possession or in someone else's, a stock enough to keep him going and to supply him with the materials and tools of his work, until he has not only finished but sold his web. This accumulation must clearly come before he can apply his industry for so long a time to such a particular business.

Just as the accumulation of stock must, in the nature of things, come before the division of labour, so labour can be subdivided further and further only in proportion as stock has first been accumulated further and further. The quantity of materials that the same number of people can work up grows greatly as labour comes to be more and more subdivided; and as each workman's operations are gradually reduced to greater simplicity, a variety of new machines come to be invented to make those operations easier and quicker. So as the division of labour advances, in order to keep an equal number of workmen constantly employed, an equal stock of provisions, and a greater stock of materials and tools than would have been needed in a cruder state of things, must be accumulated in advance. But the number of workmen in every branch of business generally grows with the division of labour in that branch; or rather, it is the growth in their number that enables them to group and subdivide themselves in this way.

Just as the accumulation of stock is needed in advance to carry on this great improvement in the productive powers of labour, so that accumulation naturally leads to this improvement. The person who employs his stock in maintaining labour necessarily wishes to employ it in such a way as to produce as great a quantity of work as possible. He therefore tries both to divide the work among his workmen in the most suitable way and to supply them with the best machines he can either invent or afford to buy. His ability to do both these things is generally in proportion to the size of his stock, or to the number of people it can employ. So the quantity of industry not only grows in every country with the growth of the stock that employs it, but, as a result of that growth, the same quantity of industry produces a much greater quantity of work.
Such, in general, are the effects of the growth of stock upon industry and its productive powers.

In the following book, I have tried to explain the nature of stock, the effects of its accumulation into capital of different kinds, and the effects of the different uses of those capitals. This book is divided into five chapters. In the first chapter, I have tried to show what are the different parts or branches into which the stock, whether of an individual or of a great society, naturally divides itself. In the second, I have tried to explain the nature and operation of money, considered as a particular branch of the general stock of society. The stock accumulated into a capital may either be employed by the person it belongs to, or it may be lent to someone else. In the third and fourth chapters, I have tried to examine how it operates in both these situations. The fifth and last chapter deals with the different effects that the different uses of capital immediately produce upon the quantity both of national industry and of the annual produce of land and labour.
